title: UPDATED: Chinese Carrier Strike Group Heads to South China Sea After Philippine Sea Drills
zh_title: 更新：中国航母战斗群在菲律宾海上演习后前往南海
summary: 2026 年 10 月 14 日，中国海军辽宁舰（16 号）在菲律宾海。日本联合参谋部照片 据日本联合参谋部称，中国人民解放军海军辽宁舰航母战斗群周三在菲律宾海进行演习，然后于周四驶向南海。由 CNS 辽宁号航空母舰 (16) 率领的打击群被发现位于日本石垣岛以南 155 英里处，正在发射和回收飞机。 JSO称，辽宁舰周三共进行了10次起降战斗机和直升机
content:
2026 年 10 月 14 日，中国海军辽宁舰（16 号）在菲律宾海。日本联合参谋部照片 据日本联合参谋部称，中国人民解放军海军辽宁舰航母战斗群周三在菲律宾海进行演习，然后于周四驶向南海。由 CNS 辽宁号航空母舰 (16) 率领的打击群被发现位于日本石垣岛以南 155 英里处，正在发射和回收飞机。 JSO周四表示，周三辽宁号舰载战斗机和直升机共起降10次。该打击群包括辽宁舰、鞍山号巡洋舰（103艘）和无锡号巡洋舰（104艘）以及怀宁号驱逐舰（123艘）。据联合特种作战司令部称，周四，该打击群被发现进入吕宋海峡，前往南中国海。日本海上自卫队驱逐舰 JS Yugiri (DD-153) 跟踪中国海军南海舰队。 JSO此前于当地时间周二上午11点观察到辽宁舰在东海向南航行，距离端上群岛西南约242英里。周三，该打击群在冲绳和宫古岛之间向东南航行，进入菲律宾海。周二和周三，日本海上自卫队的一架 P-1 海上巡逻机“夕雾”号和一架日本海上自卫队的 P-3C 猎户座 MPA 对辽宁舰进行了监视和信息收集。为了应对航母的战斗机行动，日本航空自卫队紧急出动战斗机。
辽宁舰航母战斗群包括辽宁号、巡洋舰鞍山号（103）、无锡号巡洋舰（104）以及驱逐舰怀宁号（123）。该航母战斗群于2026年10月14日在菲律宾海被发现。日本联合参谋部照片 根据中国海军的说法，南海大队正在西太平洋地区进行例行训练，不针对任何特定国家或目标。解放军海军新闻稿称：“10月14日，中国海军派遣辽宁舰编队赴西太平洋海域进行训练，此次训练是按照年度例行训练计划组织的，旨在检验和提高编队实战训练水平，不断增强执行任务能力。符合相关国际法和惯例，不针对任何特定国家和目标。”辽宁舰的第二次部署是在美国和日本即将开始双边“利剑27”演习的五天前进行的。“利剑27”联合综合反舰作战训练活动将在两个地点进行：四国以南和九州以东的地区以及从九州西南部延伸到冲绳岛东北部的地区。据日本《朝日新闻》报道，美国海军西奥多·罗斯福号航母战斗群预计将参加“利剑”演习。
海军陆战队将在石垣岛和与那国岛部署海军陆战队远征舰拦截系统（NMESIS）和TPS-80雷达。日本陆上自卫队将在石垣岛部署12型和88型机动地基地对地导弹系统，并在与那国岛部署88型，用于“利剑”非实弹射击训练。日本联合参谋部于 2026 年 10 月 14 日追踪的辽宁舰航母打击群航线地图。 日本联合参谋部地图 辽宁舰当前位置位于台湾南端以东以及台湾与菲律宾之间的吕宋海峡。自从

【原文 English Original】
PLAN aircraft carrier CNS Liaoning (16) in the Philippine Sea on Oct. 14, 2026. Japan Joint Staff Office photo The People’s Liberation Army Navy Liaoning Carrier Strike Group conducted drills in the Philippine Sea on Wednesday before sailing towards the South China Sea on Thursday, according to Japan’s Joint Staff Office. Led by aircraft carrier CNS Liaoning (16), the strike group was spotted 155 miles south of Japan’s Ishigaki Island launching and recovering aircraft. Liaoning conducted a total of 10 take-offs and landings of its embarked fighter aircraft and helicopters on Wednesday, the JSO said on Thursday. The strike group includes Liaoning, cruisers CNS Anshan (103) and CNS Wuxi (104) and destroyer CNS Huainen (123). On Thursday, the strike group was spotted entering the Luzon Strait heading towards the South China Sea, according to the JSO. Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force destroyer JS Yugiri (DD-153) shadowed the PLAN CSG. The JSO previously observed the Liaoning CSG at 11 a.m. local time Tuesday sailing south in the East China Sea around 242 miles southwest of the Danjo Islands. On Wednesday, the strike group sailed southeast between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the Philippine Sea. Yugiri , a JMSDF P-1 Maritime Patrol Aircraft and a JMSDF P-3C Orion MPA carried out surveillance and information gathering on the Liaoning CSG on Tuesday and Wednesday. In response to the carrier’s fighter operations, the Japan Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighter aircraft. The Liaoning Carrier Strike Group includes Liaoning, cruisers CNS Anshan (103) and CNS Wuxi (104) and destroyer CNS Huainen (123). The group was spotted Oct. 14, 2026, in the Philippine Sea. Japan Joint Staff Office photo According to the PLAN, the CSG is conducting routine training in the Western Pacific that is not directed at any specific country or target. “On October 14, the Chinese PLA Navy sent the Liaoning Carrier task group to the waters of the Western Pacific to conduct training, which is organized in accordance with annual routine training plan, aiming to test and improve the group’s realistic training level and continuously enhance the capabilities to execute missions. It is in compliance with relevant international law and practices and not directed against any specific country or target,” reads the PLAN news release . The Liaoning CSG’s deployment, the second for the year, comes five days before the U.S. and Japan are set to begin bilateral exercise Keen Sword 27. The joint integrated anti-ship combat training event for Keen Sword will take place in two locations – in an area south of Shikoku and east of Kyushu and in an area that stretches southwest of Kyushu up to north east of Okinawa. The U.S. Navy’s Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group is expected to take part in Keen Sword, Japanese newspaper Asahi Shimbun reported . The Marine Corps will deploy the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS) and TPS-80 radars to Ishigaki Island and Yonaguni Island. The Japan Ground Self-Defense Force will deploy its Type 12 and Type 88 mobile, ground-based, surface-to-surface missile systems on Ishigaki Island and the Type 88 on Yonaguni for non-live fire training for Keen Sword. Map of the Liaoning Carrier Strike Group’s route, tracked by Japan’s Joint Staff Office on Oct. 14, 2026. Japan Joint Staff Office map The Liaoning CSG’s current location is east of the southern tip of Taiwan and the Luzon Strait between Taiwan and the Philippines. Since Thursday, China has been conducting a series of military drills along its coast in five areas, from the South China Sea up to the northeastern province of Liaoning. None of the drills are being held around Taiwan. The drills are being held in phases and are set to conclude on Saturday. Taiwan President Lai Ching-te in his Independence Day speech on Oct. 11 said that China continues to apply pressure through military and gray-zone activities in an attempt to alter the status quo across the Taiwan Strait. “Our aim by increasing investment in national defense is not to provoke; rather, it is to deter war. We are strengthening our self-defense not to abandon dialogue, but to ensure that dialogue can take place on the basis of parity and dignity,” Lai said. “Taiwan cherishes peace, but we will not give up our freedom. We are open to exchanges, but will not accept subordination.” Lai’s speech was denounced by China Ministry of National Defense spokesperson Snr. Col. Chen Xi. “The PLA’s routine military exercises around Taiwan are a natural and justifiable way to deter any reckless actions by ‘Taiwan independence’ advocates and attempts at foreign interference, and to safeguard the safety and well-being of the Taiwanese people,” said Chen, according to a transcript . China has not announced any drills around Taiwan in response to Lai’s speech. The PLAN has not said how long the Liaoning CSG will be deployed or where it will operate. The Liaoning CSG previously carried out a 40-day deployment from May to June, returning to its homeport of Qingdao on June 22.

title: 国会议员麦戈文先生给国务卿卢比奥先生和国土安全部关于陈伟杰的信（译文）
summary: 關於中國民主人權聯盟總部副主席陳偉傑案 October 7, 2026 尊敬的國土安全部長 Markwayne Mullin 先生 尊敬的國務卿 Marco Rubio 先生 2707 Martin Luther King Jr. Ave SE 2201 C Street, NW Washington, DC 20528 Washington, D.C. 20520 原因：關於陳偉傑（Chen, Wei-Jie）的拘留及庇護案件 尊敬的 Mullin 部長與 Rubio 國務
content: 關於中國民主人權聯盟總部副主席陳偉傑案 October 7, 2026 尊敬的國土安全部長 Markwayne Mullin 先生 尊敬的國務卿 Marco Rubio 先生 2707 Martin Luther King Jr. Ave SE 2201 C Street, NW Washington, DC 20528 Washington, D.C. 20520 原因：關於陳偉傑（Chen, Wei-Jie）的拘留及庇護案件 尊敬的 Mullin 部長與 Rubio 國務卿： 我致函表達對陳偉傑（Chen, Wei-Jie）被拘留一事的嚴重關切；他目前被美國移民與海關執法局 （ICE）拘押於亞利桑那州埃洛伊（Eloy）的埃洛伊拘留中心。我謹敦促當局立即釋放他，公平 且及時地審理其庇護或其他形式保護的申請；同時，無論在何種情況下，都不得將其遣返回中華 人民共和國，也不得將其遣送至可能最終導致其被送回中國的第三國。 陳先生自 2025 年 9 月起一直處於 ICE 的拘押之下。他於 2023 年抵達美國，並在入境時明確向 邊境巡邏人員表達了尋求政治庇護的意願。 陳先生曾居住於香港，並積極參與了「反對修訂逃犯條例」運動，這使他被香港當局視為批評人 士。自抵達美國以來，他持續公開反對中國共產黨的一黨專政，並繼續參與推動中國民主、人權 及公民社會的活動。 身為美國眾議院湯姆·蘭托斯人權委員會（Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission）的聯合主 席，以及國會及行政當局中國委員會（CECC）的成員兼前任主席（曾與時任參議員的 Marco Rubio 共事），我可以證實，民主派人士正遭受中華人民共和國當局的嚴厲迫害。 CECC（美國 國會及行政當局中國委員會）的年度報告1 詳盡記錄了此類侵權行為，美國國務院發布的《各國人權報告》亦是如此。 我深信，鑑於陳先生公開持有的政治立場，一旦被遣返回中國，他將面臨遭受迫害的嚴重風險── 包括被拘留及遭受嚴厲懲罰。他應當獲釋，脫離美國移民與海關執法局（ICE）的拘押，並免於 被遣返回中國的風險。此外，在審議陳先生的庇護申請時，我敦促政府以公正且嚴肅的態度，考 慮所有重要及相關因素，包括中國的人權狀況記錄，以及陳先生回國後將面臨的嚴重風險。 1 https://www.cecc.gov/publications/annual-reports 非常感謝您的關注。 謹啟 麥戈文（James P. McGovern） 國會議員

【大纪元2026年10月11日讯】（大纪元记者林丹纽约报导）10月10日是中华民国115年双十国庆，一群来自中国大陆的移民一早在纽约法拉盛图书馆前，举行庄严的“青天白日满地红旗”升旗仪式，庆祝中华民国成立115周年。他们挥舞中华民国国旗与美国国旗，表达盼望中国大陆早日实现民主、自由与宪政的心声。 2026年10月10日，大陆移民在纽约华人社区法拉盛庆祝中华民国115年国庆，举行庄严的升旗仪式，盼中国大陆有一天实现宪政民主。（中华民国国军老兵关爱中心提供） 大陆移民在纽约法拉盛举行中华民国115年国庆升旗典礼，盼中国大陆实现宪政民主。（中华民国老兵关爱中心提供） 活动由中华民国公民联盟、中华民国国军老兵关爱中心主办，参加的有中国新时代人民党、基督徒公义联盟、中国民主人权联盟等团体，这些团体的成员多为大陆新移民。参加者打出横幅：“中华民国才是我的国，中共国是非法国”、“解散中国共产党，台湾接管新中国，恢复中华民国，普用台湾宪法 ”。众人高喊口号：“结束中共暴政！中华民国万岁！” 在美国国歌和中华民国国歌之后，在中华民国国旗歌声中，青天白日满地红旗冉冉升起。 活动主持人、中华民国国军老兵关爱中心执行长王莉在开场时表示，升起中华民国国旗，“是对自由中国的希望，对民族共和的信念，对中华民国未来的期待。” 她说，中国大陆不仅要结束中共一党专政，更重要的是建立一个自由、民主、法治的国家，“中华民国的历史与宪政制度，可以为中国大陆未来的政治转型提供重要参考。” 中华民国海外公民委员会执行长曹胜华表示，根据《中华民国宪法增修条文》的表述，在国家统一前，中华民国分为大陆地区和自由地区（台湾）。他说：“中国大陆是战区、是匪区、是敌占区、是沦陷区”，庆祝双十国庆之际，不应忘记中国大陆的同胞，期盼中国大陆早日结束中共统治，走向民主宪政。 曹胜华并指出，台湾（中华民国）因此不仅在地缘政治上是美国的战略重地，也是美国反共产主义意识形态的前线，他说：“2026 年美国独立 250 周年庆典上，川普总统将共产主义对美国与世界的危害当成演讲的核心主题：‘共产主义是世界上一切自由人民的敌人，是美国宪法的敌人，更是 1776 年 7月4日的敌人。’美国永远不会成为共产主义国家，而中华民国大陆沦陷区必将终结共产主义的奴役，回归民主宪政道路。” 中华民国国军老兵关爱中心董事长胡福庆表示，他长期坚持街头宣讲国军在抗日战争中的贡献，是希望更多华人，尤其是被中共洗脑的大陆移民重新认识中华民国的过去、现在与未来。他也希望大陆民众看到，中共政权结束之后，中国并非只能面对混乱、分裂或另一场专制，“回归共和、重建宪政的中华民国，是可以追循的一条道路。” 中国新民党创办人杨茂森则以“民国魂”为主题发言，回顾中华民国建立及抗日战争的历史，他并批评中共对台湾的施压与跨国镇压行为。 针对近日发生的加州华裔房产中介张婉莹监控台湾总统赖清德长子一案，杨茂森表示：“这不是一般的跨国镇压案件，如果中共不承认台湾是一个国家，承认它属于中华民国管辖，那么这个案件是跨国镇压；但如果中共认为台湾是一个主权国家，那么对台湾这个主权国家的总统的儿子的监控，那属于侵略行为，性质就不一样了。所以，我们要把中共的残暴、反人类揭露出来，同时要终结它。” 中华民国公民联盟总协特助凯武说，民主的先驱不是哪些老而腐朽的人，他们是年轻、正直、能明辨是非的人；现在的年轻人也应该挺身而出，成为中国民主的栋梁。而当今的中国，人民不能自由表达意见、没有选举权，正如孙中山先生所说的：“革命尚未成功， 同志仍须努力”。 中国民主人权联盟纽约副主席钱家发回顾历史说：“中共邪党为了阻止蒋委员长‘攘外必先安内’的剿共策略，竟然诱骗张学良发动西安事变，此后，中共邪党在共同抗日的幌子下，‘七分发展，二分应付，一分抗日’，利用国民党在抗战中的军力消耗，在苏俄的支持下，再一次发动内战，将中华民国政府逼退至台湾。” 来自南京的钱家发说，他对中华民国的记忆刻在骨子里，“从总统府、国民大会堂、内政部、外交部、中山陵，以及道路两旁高大的梧桐树，总想像着中华民国有那么一天会还都南京。” 他表示，中华民国在台湾维持民主制度，成为中国大陆民众向往自由的一座灯塔。 基督徒公义联盟代表赵西玲说：“我们希望有一天，中国人民能够自由表达意见、自由选择信仰，能够在法律面前人人平等，让权力受到制度的约束，让公义成为社会的根基。” 国军老兵关爱中心代表杨家儒表示，当中国大陆迎来政治转型的历史时刻，重新走上中华民国的宪政道路，是值得考虑的选择。 众人在赵西玲的带领下大合唱《中华民国颂》。法拉盛缅街熙熙攘攘，升旗仪式吸引众多大陆移民驻足观看。 责任编辑：黄小堂

title: A Taiwanese Youth’s Perspective: TSMC’s US Expansion and the American Dream

content:
下载全文 PDF 台湾积体电路制造公司 (TSMC，台湾积体电路制造公司) 生产 90% 以上的先进芯片，为人工智能开发提供动力，显着提升了台湾在全球事务中的战略重要性。近年来，认知影响力行动仍然加剧了许多台湾老年人的担忧，担心台积电的海外扩张可能会损害台湾的经济利益、战略影响力和才华横溢的工程师。然而，像我这样的台湾年轻人可能会认为这些担忧被夸大了。台积电一再强调，其最先进的研发能力将留在台湾，台湾将继续作为公司技术开发和全球生产网络的核心。台湾人不应该担心台积电在美国扩大生产，主要有以下三个原因。首先，此次扩张使台积电能够更好地服务美国领先客户并增加其商机。其次，将生产从台湾转移出去有助于减少环境压力和地缘政治风险，并增强半导体供应链的稳定性。最后，台积电的国际发展计划增强了台湾的全球影响力，并加强了与世界各地合作伙伴的联系。
市场准入、政府补贴和下游供应链效益尽管人们对台积电在美国工厂建造和生产半导体的高成本存在合理的担忧，但值得承认这项活动的长期好处：使台积电能够更快地接触全球客户。尽管在海外建立业务需要更高的成本，但这种扩张在财务上已被证明是可行的，正如台积电亚利桑那州所证明的那样。仅 2025 年，亚利桑那州晶圆厂的净利润就达到新台币 42.​​32 亿元（1.358 亿美元），乍一看似乎是全年数据，但实际上仅在一个季度内就实现了这一收入。台积电亚利桑那州取得成功的关键原因之一是全球芯片市场的变化。美国主要依赖台湾制造尖端逻辑芯片。通过在美国建设更多晶圆厂，台积电能够更好地满足其主要客户的产能需求，其中包括AMD、苹果、英伟达和高通等美国公司。这可以实现更快、更个性化的客户服务，从而与大公司建立信任和亲和力，并鼓励他们将来从台积电购买产品。除了贴近客户之外，美国政府还积极利用立法来鼓励半导体公司在国内建设。
美国商务部根据 CHIPS 和科学法案向台积电提供 66 亿美元的直接拨款资金，并获得 50 亿美元的低息联邦贷款。这笔资金有助于抵消美国比台湾更高的建设和运营成本。此外，台积电在美国的扩张不仅建立了跨行业联系，还为长春集团和三立化学等台湾重要供应商在美国运营铺平了道路，从而推动了广泛的芯片生态系统。当这些主力晶圆厂搬迁到新的土地时，整个材料供应网络也随之移动，从而带来更多的商机。通过授权这些供应商扩展到全球市场，此类行动最终会改变

DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF Producing more than 90 percent of the advanced chips powering AI development, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC, 台灣積體電路製造公司) has significantly elevated Taiwan’s strategic importance in global affairs. In recent years, cognitive influence operations have nonetheless fueled fears among many older Taiwanese that TSMC’s overseas expansion could cost Taiwan economic benefits, strategic leverage, and talented engineers. Younger Taiwanese like myself, however, may see these concerns as overstated. TSMC has repeatedly emphasized that its most advanced research and development (R&D) capabilities will remain in Taiwan, and that the island will continue to serve as the heart of the company’s technology development and global production network. Taiwanese should not be concerned about TSMC expanding its production in the United States for three main reasons. Firstly, this expansion allows TSMC to better serve leading-edge US customers and grow its business opportunities. Secondly, diversifying production away from Taiwan helps reduce environmental strains and geopolitical risks, and strengthens the stability of the semiconductor supply chain. Finally, TSMC’s international development plans enhance Taiwan’s global presence and strengthen connections with partners around the world. Market Access, Government Subsidies, and Downstream Supply Chain Benefits Although there are valid concerns about the high cost of building and producing semiconductors at TSMC facilities in the United States, it is worth acknowledging the long-term benefit of this activity: providing TSMC with quicker access to customers worldwide. Even though establishing operations abroad entails higher costs, this expansion has proven financially viable, as demonstrated by TSMC Arizona. In 2025 alone, the Arizona fab recorded a net income of NTD 4.232 billion (USD 135.8 million) —income that, at first glance, may appear to have been full-year data, but was actually made in just one quarter. One key reason why TSMC Arizona has been successful has been changes in the global market for chips. The United States relies primarily on Taiwan for the fabrication of leading-edge logic chips. By building more fabs in the United States, TSMC is better able to satisfy the capacity demands of its key customers, including American companies such as AMD, Apple, Nvidia, and Qualcomm, among others. This enables faster, more personalized customer service, which builds trust and affinity with large companies and encourages them to buy from TSMC in the future. Beyond customer proximity, the United States government has actively employed legislation to encourage semiconductor companies to build domestically. The US Department of Commerce has awarded TSMC USD 6.6 billion in direct grant funding under the CHIPS and Science Act , along with access to USD 5 billion in low-interest federal loans. This funding helps offset the higher costs of construction and operation in the US compared to Taiwan. Furthermore, TSMC’s American expansion not only builds cross-industry connections, but it also drives a broad chip ecosystem by paving the way for critical Taiwanese suppliers such as the Chang Chun Group and Sunlit Chemical to operate in the United States. When these anchor fabs move to new land, the entire material supply network also moves with them, leading to more business opportunities. By empowering these suppliers to expand into global markets, such actions ultimately transfer international investment back into Taiwan’s domestic economy. Therefore, continued expansion in the United States represents a strategic investment in TSMC’s long-term financial future. Image: TSMC Fab 21 under construction in Phoenix, Arizona (November 2023). (Image source: Wikimedia Commons ) Environmental Risks and Geopolitics In order to maintain satisfying relationships with customers, TSMC must operate a stable and unbroken semiconductor production line. Some Taiwanese believe that this stability can be maintained at home, yet growing environmental risks and geopolitical realities indicate that relying on production in Taiwan alone is increasingly fragile. Within this context, TSMC’s expansion to the United States can help maintain a stable semiconductor production line. As TSMC continues to expand its production capacity, Taiwan is gradually reaching the limits of its environmental carrying capacity. Semiconductor fabs consume vast amounts of water and electricity. Building more and more fabs in Taiwan will put too much pressure on the power grid. Increasing load will risk energy shortages and infrastructure strain, thus destabilizing production lines not only for TSMC but also for other businesses in Taiwan. By contrast, locations for TSMC’s expansion, such as Arizona, possess far more abundant resources. Arizona has one of the biggest energy grids in the United States, operating over 6,551 megawatts (MW) of installed solar capacity alongside nearly 3,900 megawatts (MW) of battery energy storage systems. Beyond electricity, water is also essential for the semiconductor industry; a single advanced chip factory can consume up to 38 million liters of water per day (an amount approximately equivalent to the daily water usage of a medium-sized city). As a small island with finite resources, Taiwan simply lacks the physical capacity to sustain such immense environmental pressure. Crowding the nation with dozens of new factories would push its fragile water supply to a dangerous breaking point, placing a burden on the everyday lives of Taiwanese citizens. Moreover, an earthquake that hit eastern Taiwan in 2024 caused TSMC factories in Tainan to shut down temporarily, as chip fabs are designed to automatically cease production when any tremors occur. For instance, EUV chipmaking machines possess sensors that detect infinitesimal movements that cannot be noticed by humans; if the EUV machine senses the floor moving, it will shut down completely. Indeed, continuing to print during tremors can blur the circuit lines and potentially result in significant financial losses as wafers must be discarded. Hence, moving factories to locations like Arizona helps mitigate natural disaster risks such as earthquakes and provides a more controllable environment, rendering chip production lines more efficient. Given the relative availability of land, water, and electrical resources in North America, building factories in the United States may ultimately be beneficial for maintaining the stability of the Taiwanese production lines. By expanding its manufacturing capacity overseas, TSMC can reduce its exposure to geopolitical risks – and, in the event of war, help sustain the industrial capacity of the “arsenal of democracy.” For more than seven decades , Taiwan has faced persistent tensions across the Taiwan Strait, which have intensified in recent years and created significant geopolitical uncertainty. A war in the Taiwan Strait could severely disrupt global semiconductor supply chains, triggering shortages of advanced chips and inflicting trillions of dollars in economic losses worldwide. If key fabs in Taiwan are damaged or destroyed, rebuilding the lost production capacity could take years. By expanding its manufacturing capacity into the United States, TSMC can help key geopolitical partners like America maintain access to chips during wartime situations. Soft Power and Continuity Many Taiwanese argue that TSMC is the “ silicon shield ” protecting Taiwan against China. Therefore, they claim that the protection of this shield would be forfeited should TSMC build more factories in the United States. However, I believe TSMC’s global expansion can also help Taiwan garner greater international recognition by building stronger connections with local communities overseas. One example is the collaboration between Japan Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing (JASM) and the TSMC Education and Culture Foundation, which brought Taiwan’s OneSong Orchestra to Kumamoto for a cultural concert . When locals connect with Taiwanese culture through these activities, it transforms Taiwan from an unfamiliar chip supplier into a culturally rich nation that bonds with local communities on a personal level. Such community bonds naturally encourage local communities to support strong diplomatic ties between their government and that of Taiwan. Additionally, these community investments extend into classrooms, where local universities partner with TSMC to build a new generation of semiconductor professionals who have been trained through Taiwanese resources. In the context of Japan, cultural exchanges between TSMC and the local community not only strengthen the company’s ties with Kumamoto residents, but also help build public support for its overseas expansion. In this sense, TSMC’s overseas expansion does more than diversify production—it can also expand Taiwan’s international presence and strengthen its ties with key partners around the world. Many Taiwanese refer to TSMC as the nation’s “Guardian Mountain” (護國神山) because of its crucial role in safeguarding Taiwan’s economic prosperity and national security. TSMC’s global expansion can strengthen the resilience of the semiconductor supply chain, bring production closer to its customers, expand its business opportunities, create new possibilities for young Taiwanese, and enhance Taiwan’s international presence. Some Taiwanese elders may worry that sending engineers to the United States represents a loss of human resources for Taiwan. However, these Taiwanese engineers are not abandoning Taiwan. Instead, they are stepping into global leadership roles and establishing important cross-border industry networks. When these professionals eventually return to Taiwan, they will be able to train the next generation of engineers preparing to go overseas and advance Taiwan’s economic prosperity. Expanding into the United States, therefore, does not mark the end of TSMC’s role as Taiwan’s “Guardian Mountain.” Rather, it is a pragmatic step toward ensuring that TSMC can continue to fulfill that role in a rapidly changing world. One Youth’s Perspective As a junior in the International Bilingual School at Hsinchu-Science-Park, many of my classmates’ parents are employed at TSMC. Drawing inspiration from their parents, some have also decided to pursue a career at TSMC. The establishment of TSMC Arizona has encouraged even more of them to pursue this track, and many of my peers are excited about the new job opportunities abroad that have been created. Indeed, these new job opportunities appeal to Taiwanese teenagers who had never yet been able to imagine their part in the “American Dream.” Ironically, according to a 2024 ABC News/Ipsos survey of US adults, public confidence in the American Dream has significantly eroded. Yet, new TSMC subsidiaries in the United States not only stabilize the production chain but also help revive the long-faded “American Dream” for Taiwanese youth. The main point: While many commentators in Taiwan suggest that TSMC’s expansion to the United States weakens Taiwan’s economic and national security, the business decisions may actually prove more economically viable, and relieve pressure on Taiwan’s grid and water supply. Meanwhile, the opportunities to work in the United States revive the long-faded “American Dream” among Taiwanese youth. title: Fruit at the Forefront of a Trade and Diplomatic Push
zh_title: 处于贸易和外交推动前沿的水果
source: 华盛顿全球台湾研究中心

下载全文 PDF 今年，来自台湾的新鲜水果首次出现在英国和法国的超市货架上，这让英国和法国的购物者大饱眼福。第一批来自台南的优质欧文芒果和来自台中的黑叶荔枝混合装运，已于六月初在英国曼彻斯特清关。此后不久，台湾芒果也抵达法国，尽管每颗芒果的售价高达29美元，但仍深受法国消费者的欢迎。不到一个月的时间，四吨多的水果就被卖光了。获得将台湾产品运送到欧洲高度保护的关税区的官方许可是一个复杂的过程。该地区与农产品相关的进口法规具有严格的限制性，因为它们涵盖了从标签和农药暴露到农产品如何销售等各个方面。因此，经过“多年的谈判和技术准备”，台北驻欧盟和比利时代表处于2025年宣布获得芒果和番石榴进口清关，这是一项伟大的成就。八个月后，荔枝和火龙果获得批准。欧洲并不是台湾水果出口唯一面临挑战的目的地。台湾农业部门的官员也寻求向新西兰出口菠萝。
这一努力始于2013年新西兰与台澎金马单独关税区经济合作协定（ANZTEC，纽西兰与台澎金马关税领域经济合作定）的签署。经过八年的ANZTEC修正案双边谈判，新西兰终于打开了优质台湾菠萝的大门。 2025年5月，即ANZTEC修订案获得批准两年后，第一批台湾菠萝抵达新西兰市场。减少对单一市场的依赖 2010 年，台湾加入世界贸易组织 (WTO) 前后，台湾的水果开始在许多传统市场失去竞争力，其中包括日本和菲律宾。随着台湾农业面临新的国际竞争，海峡两岸经济合作框架协议（ECFA，海峡两岸经济合作架构协议）为台湾水果创造了机会，导致对单一市场中国的出口大幅增长。 ECFA是送给台湾农民的一份礼物。颁布两年后，台湾农产品出口总额增长了百分之八以上。其中，对中国的水果出口增长了42%；香蕉、哈密瓜、柠檬、红火龙果等早期收获清单上的农产品比2007年猛增42%。然而，受ECFA保护的农产品贸易并没有持续太久。
2021 年 2 月和 9 月，中国突然停止从台湾进口——首先是菠萝，然后是糖苹果和莲雾——声称检查中在多批货物中发现了柑橘粉蚧。 ECFA 批评者表示，中国本来就不是一个可行的长期市场。中国开始种植和培育曾经是台湾标志性水果的水果，侵蚀了对台湾出口的需求。此外，北京开始利用进口水果作为象征性的大棒来迫使台湾就范。中华经济研究院颜慧欣曾警告台湾有必要减少对中国市场的依赖，她写道：“

【原文 English Original】
DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF Shoppers in the United Kingdom and France got a treat when supplies of fresh fruit from Taiwan found their way onto their supermarket shelves for the first time this year . The first batch, a mixed shipment of premium Irwin mangoes from Tainan and black-leaf lychees from Taichung, cleared customs in the British city of Manchester in early June. Taiwan’s mangoes also arrived in France shortly thereafter , enjoying overwhelming popularity among French consumers despite the astonishing price tag of $29 USD per fruit. In less than a month, more than four tons of the fruit were sold out. Getting an official permit to send Taiwan produce into Europe’s highly protected customs area is a complicated process. The region’s produce-related import regulations are highly restrictive, as they cover everything ranging from labelling and pesticide exposure, to how the produce can be marketed . Therefore, it marked a great achievement when the Taipei Representative Office in the European Union (EU) and Belgium announced in 2025 that it had received clearance for mango and guava imports , after “years of negotiations and technical preparations.” Approvals for lychees and dragon fruit followed eight months later. Europe was not the only challenging destination for Taiwan’s fruit exports. Taiwan’s officials in agricultural sectors also sought to export pineapples to New Zealand. The endeavor began with the signing of the Agreement between New Zealand and the Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen, and Matsu on Economic Cooperation (ANZTEC, 紐西蘭與臺澎金馬個別關稅領域經濟合作協 定) in 2013. Eight years of bilateral negotiations on the amendments to ANZTEC finally opened New Zealand’s doors to premium Taiwan pineapples. In May of 2025—two years after the ANZTEC revisions were approved—the first batch of Taiwan’s pineapples arrived in the New Zealand market. Reducing Dependence on a Single Market In 2010, around the time of Taiwan’s accession into the World Trade Organization (WTO), the island’s fruit began losing competitiveness in many of its traditional markets, which included Japan and the Philippines . As Taiwan’s agricultural industry scrambled in the face of new international competition, the Cross Straits Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement (ECFA, 海峽兩岸經濟合作架構協 議) created an opportunity for Taiwan’s fruit, resulting in a huge jump in exports into a single market : China. ECFA was a gift for Taiwanese farmers. Two years after it was promulgated, Taiwan’s total agricultural exports increased more than eight percent. Particularly, fruit exports to China grew 42 percent; and produce on the early harvest list, such as bananas, hami melons, lemons, and red dragon fruits, surged 42 percent compared to 2007. Nevertheless, the agricultural trade protected by ECFA did not last. In February and September 2021, China abruptly ended its imports from Taiwan—first pineapples, then sugar apples and wax apples—claiming that inspections had discovered citrus mealybugs in a number of shipments. ECFA critics say China was not a viable long-term market to begin with. China started growing and cultivating what used to be Taiwan’s signature fruits, eroding demand for Taiwan’s exports. Additionally, Beijing began to use fruit imports as a figurative stick to bring Taiwan to heel. Huai-Shing Yen (顏慧 欣 ) of the Chung Hua Institution for Economic Research (中華經濟研究 院 ) had warned of the need to reduce Taiwan’s reliance on the Chinese market, writing that: “The high concentration structure (of exports to China) makes it certain that the import restrictions will have a commercial impact on relevant farmers in Taiwan. As such, China’s actions to restrict imports are loud reminders of the vulnerability that this ‘export dependence’ causes for these agricultural products.” Yen also warned that even if Taiwan had sought to seek redress for China’s actions through the WTO, China “would not be obliged to enter consultations or negotiations with Taiwan.” Instead, Taiwan should seek alternatives, more reliable markets for its products. Weeks after China’s sugar apple and wax apple ban, the then-Council of Agriculture (COA, 行政院農業委員會 ) announced a strategy that sought to capitalize on existing and potential demand for Taiwanese fruit both inside and outside the country. Image: Local officials in Pingtung County (southeastern Taiwan) pose with a shipment of various fruits— mangoes, lychees, and dragon fruit—bound for shipment to Europe under the terms of new trade agreements with the European Union (June 2026). (Image source: Central News Agency ) Cold Chain Logistics: The Unsung Hero Today, Taiwanese fruit is sold at a premium in supermarkets and specialty retailers in numerous countries, such as Japan, South Korea, Australia, Canada, Singapore, Hong Kong, Malaysia, Brunei and Palau—but the produce would not have made it beyond its shores without advancements in Taiwan’s cold chain logistics industry. The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI, 工業技術研究 院) , a non-government R&D organization that incubated Taiwan’s semiconductor industry , has been dedicated to the development of cold chain logistics since the 1990s . Janet Chen (陳慧 娟) , General Director of ITRI’s Service Systems Technology Center, told this author that there are similarities to transporting fruit and semiconductors, as they both have strict requirements in temperature, humidity, and cleanliness: “Agricultural products must be kept within appropriate temperature and humidity ranges to slow deterioration and preserve freshness and nutritional value. Semiconductor components may also be sensitive to temperature and humidity. Clean storage and transportation environments help prevent cross-contamination and microbial growth in agricultural cold chains. Semiconductor manufacturing requires exceptionally clean environments because even microscopic particles can cause defects.” Chen adds: “Freshness is a major source of value for agricultural products, making timely delivery essential. Semiconductor supply chains also require fast and reliable transportation because delays may lead to missed business opportunities, inventory shortages, or production disruptions. Agricultural cold chains require traceability from farm to table to support food safety and quality control.” [1] Government Ensures Taiwan’s Fruit is Compliant The Ministry of Agriculture (MOA, 農業部) has also ensured that fruit exports comply with regulations that differ from territory to territory. For instance, mangoes heading to Europe must be subjected to heat treatment to kill off any pests or microbial hitchhikers, while pineapples bound for New Zealand must be harvested at a specific life stage . This is not to mention the various pesticide standards set in overseas markets. To support Taiwan’s farmers, the MOA and local governments in 2024 inaugurated a processing park in Yujing District in Tainan , which can process mango and pineapple to meet international standards. Its Produce Processing and Cold Chain Logistics Center ( 玉井農產加工及冷鏈物流中心) is equipped with pre-cooling, processing, refrigeration, and freezer zones capable of processing as much as 800 tons of mangoes a year. External uncertainties highlight the significance of transport quality control. Kris Tang, General Manager of fruit exporter Sunray Fresh ( 昇睿鮮 農) , revealed to this author that during their first commercial shipment, fruit travelled via Frankfurt in the midst of a staffing shortage and a heat wave. “The mango and lychee could not be placed on the same onward flight to the UK and had to arrive separately. (By then), our priority was not simply to preserve the original schedule, but to protect the quality and integrity of the products.” [2] Gaining entry into Europe’s market is a good start—but more needs to be done if Taiwanese farmers are to cut their reliance on the Chinese market entirely. Focus Taiwan has reported that the Taiwan still sold USD 370 million worth of fresh fruit to Hong Kong and China from 2020 to May 2026, while exports to Japan totaled USD 199.4 million during the same period. But exporters know that getting a foothold is just the first, albeit critical step. Tang told this author: “The first shipment was important, but it was only the beginning. What matters is whether we can create a repeatable and commercially sustainable route that allows more Taiwanese fruit and agricultural products to enter the UK and, eventually, the wider European market.” [3] The main point: Taiwan’s move away from relying on a handful of traditional export markets like China has opened new doors for its fruit exports. That pivot, which also resulted in new technological innovation within Taiwan’s cold-chain logistics system, opened new markets in Europe for Taiwan’s mangoes and lychees. Developing its fruit market has also paved the way for Taiwan’s exports beyond high-tech products. [1] Author’s interview, summer 2026. [2] Author’s interview, summer 2026. [3] Ibid. The post Fruit at the Forefront of a Trade and Diplomatic Push appeared first on Global Taiwan Institute .

title: “Last Year We Needed Volunteers, This Year We Need Tourists”: Reviving Post-Disaster Tourism in Eastern Taiwan

content:
下载整期 PDF 城镇重建很久之后，它的形象可能仍停留在过去。潜在的游客可能会通过过时的图像和以前的灾难头条新闻来查看这个地方。如果没有足够的保证或激励，他们会比必要的时间更长时间地避开，忘记这个地方曾经是，而且仍然可以是一个度假胜地。这种现象给依赖旅游业为生的居民和企业带来了一场延迟的、不太明显的灾难。花莲县横跨台湾东北海岸和山谷。该地区的经济依赖旅游业，但由于历史上的自然灾害而遭受重挫。对于花莲来说，该行业约占全县就业和产值的40%。该县的光福镇经历了 2024 年地区性地震对旅游业的影响和 2025 年洪水造成的自然破坏，目前正在努力应对游客量长期低迷的问题。本文通过对当地人的采访和第一手研究，探讨了居民在灾后努力重建城镇吸引力的经历，并探讨了政府迄今为止为支持旅游业恢复所做的努力。它还详细说明了政府应采取哪些进一步措施来真正重振经济。本案例研究揭示了灾后重建的长期现实以及重振当地经济所需的政府干预规模。
这也对台湾在国际舞台上的韧性提出了更广泛的问题：当自然灾害和更广泛的危险认知威胁到旅游业时，目的地如何保持游客的信心？由头条新闻定义的小镇光复镇坐落在台湾花莲县花东裂谷，长期以来以其田园风光、自行车路线和原住民文化而闻名。花莲北部该地区的主要旅游景点太鲁阁峡谷吸引的国际游客会顺着峡谷而下，在光复寺停留欣赏风景并在附近的温泉休息。但近两年来，该地区的旅游业经受了严峻考验。 2024年4月，花莲地震给我们带来了第一波打击。太鲁阁峡谷在地震中受损严重，连接台北和花莲的高速公路暂时被封锁。全球主要新闻媒体的头版刊登了花莲市一座倒塌建筑物的图片。来台国际游客数量锐减，国内游客将假期从花莲转移到其他地方。峡谷以南的所有乡镇都受到旅游业下降的影响。尽管如此，光复并不是受灾最严重的地区之一，它位于花莲市以南一小时车程的地方。居民经历了强烈的震动，建筑物遭受了结构性影响，但受损程度并不像北部城市地区那么严重。
花莲县的大部分地区都是低层房屋，周围环绕着连绵起伏的农田和山脉。该地区很幸运，基本上避免了新闻报道中花莲市的破坏场景。然而，广泛传播的这座城市的图像让人感觉整个县都遭到了破坏，因此参观不安全。在高速公路再次向游客开放后，这个观点仍然存在很长一段时间。图片：X 上危险倾斜的天王星大厦附近的救援人员和设备

【原文 English Original】
DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF Long after a town rebuilds itself, its image can remain stuck in the past. Potential visitors may view the place through outdated images and previous disaster headlines. Without enough reassurance or incentives, they steer clear for longer than necessary, forgetting that the place was, and still can be, a holiday destination. This phenomenon results in a delayed, less visible disaster for residents and businesses whose livelihoods depend on tourism. Hualien County stretches over the northeastern coast and valleys of Taiwan. The area’s economy relies on the tourism industry, which has been set back due to a history of natural disasters. For Hualien, that sector accounts for around 40 percent of the county’s employment and output value. A township within this county, Guangfu, is grappling with a particularly prolonged downturn in visitors, having weathered both the tourism fallout of a regional earthquake in 2024 and the physical devastation of floods in 2025. Through interviews with locals and first-hand research, this piece explores the experiences of residents struggling to rebuild a town’s appeal post-disaster, and examines the government’s efforts to support tourism recovery to date. It also details what further steps the government should take to genuinely revive the economy. This case study reveals the long-term realities of post-disaster reconstruction and the scale of government intervention needed to re-energize a local economy. It also raises wider questions for Taiwan’s resilience on the international stage: how can a destination maintain visitor confidence when natural disasters—and broader perceptions of danger—threaten tourism? A Township Defined by Headlines Guangfu Township, nestled in the East Rift Valley of Hualien County, Taiwan, was long known for its rural scenery, cycling routes, and indigenous culture. International tourists drawn in by Taroko Gorge, the region’s main tourist attraction in north Hualien, would make their way down the valley, stopping by Guangfu to enjoy the view and rest in the nearby hot springs. But in the last two years, the area’s tourism industry has been severely tested. In April 2024, the Hualien earthquake dealt the first blow. Taroko Gorge was considerably damaged by the earthquake, and the highway connecting Taipei and Hualien was temporarily blocked. Images of a collapsed building in Hualien City were displayed on front pages of major global news outlets . The number of international visitors to Taiwan plummeted and domestic visitors redirected their holidays away from Hualien. No township south of the gorge was spared the impact of the drop in tourism. This said, Guangfu was not amongst the most severely damaged areas, being situated one hour south of Hualien City by car. Residents experienced strong tremors and buildings sustained structural impacts, although the extent of the damage was not as severe as in the urban areas to the north. Much of this part of Hualien County is made up of low-rise houses surrounded by rolling farmland and mountains. The region was fortunate to largely avoid the scenes of destruction in Hualien City that dominated the news. Nevertheless, the widely broadcasted images of the city contributed to a perception that the whole county was devastated and therefore unsafe to visit. This viewpoint remained long after the highway was opened to visitors again. Image: Rescue workers and equipment near the dangerously-leaning Uranus Building on Xuanyuan Road in Hualien City, in the immediate aftermath of the April 3, 2024 Hualien earthquake. (Image source: ROC Presidential Office / Wikimedia Commons ) In 2024, the National Tourism Administration (交通部觀光署) offered subsidies for six months following the earthquake , in order to stimulate tourism recovery in Hualien. This included the “Hualien Independent Travel Accommodation Subsidy” (花蓮自由行住宿補助) , featuring an NTD 1000 (around USD 30) rebate on the first night, with an additional NTD 1500 (around USD 47) provided on the second. This was combined with discounts on charter flights , shuttles , amusement parks and local products. With Taroko Gorge still shut, the county government diversified regional branding, releasing the video, “ On the Way to Eastern Taiwan: Travel Freely with Peace of Mind , ” and hosting international marketing shows alongside local spotlight events such as the 2024 World Bicycle Day. These initiatives reportedly helped tourism activities in Hualien reach pre-earthquake rates from 2025 , though it is unclear what proportion of these numbers trickled down to townships in the south, such as Guangfu. However, in September 2025, just as tourists were returning to the region, Guangfu Township faced a second blow which left a more devastating impact to the community. The overflowing of a nearby barrier lake caused flash floods, which sent mud and debris into homes and businesses. The floods also left many stranded after a lack of comprehensive evacuation notices caught locals off guard. Fellow citizens arrived in extraordinary numbers to aid in cleanup efforts, with an estimated 30,000 volunteers appearing on September 27, and tens of thousands more in the following weeks. Li Jen-i (李仁義), the owner of breakfast shop Yonghe Doujiang (永和豆漿) in Guangfu, recalls their arrival after his shop’s cooking equipment had been washed away: “It brings tears to my eyes to remember. The warmth of Taiwanese people, you never forget that.” [1] The government emergency response was swift. The Legislative Yuan (立法院) passed a NTD 27 billion (USD 859 million) special budget to rebuild parts of the township damaged by the floods, and offered temporary housing, reconstruction loans, and cleanup subsidies to victims. The county government dispatched 790 mud removal trucks and cooperated with the bike rental company YouBike to temporarily install bike stations . When I visited a year later, the relief efforts of both government and private charities had significantly reduced the physical damage of the floods. Many businesses have reopened and locals await the return of visitors. But now, a less visible crisis is unfolding in Guangfu. Many tourists still skip the township, deterred by the lingering perception that conditions there are wet and muddy at best, or dangerous at worst. Ongoing disaster-related reporting continues to dominate the media, re-enforcing the perception of Guangfu as a township still in devastation. Locals are therefore struggling to keep their businesses afloat. Rebuilding public confidence in the township as a tourist destination is a challenge residents cannot shoulder alone. It will require a different kind of targeted, strategic support from the government. Image: An ant art installation in Danongdafu Flatland Forest Park (Image source: Author’s photograph) Tourist Restoration Policies Beyond Physical Recovery Two challenges remain when it comes to sustainably revitalizing Guangfu’s economy. First, government funding in Guangfu has so far prioritized the concrete efforts of physical restoration over the more abstract needs of tourism recovery. The initial response to the floods by both the central and county governments was remarkable in both speed and scale, with much of Guangfu’s physical infrastructure restored in under a year. Now, government support should extend beyond emergency relief and employ a strategic approach to sustaining the long-term survival of local industries. “People might have their homes again, but what can they do with no livelihood? We need further government support to promote the township and help our businesses get back on their feet,” says “Uncle Tien” ( 田克靚 ), owner of Uncle Tien’s Guesthouse ( 見青小築民宿) , whose monthly revenue has been down by 50-80 percent since the autumn of 2025. [2] Second, Guangfu has received limited visibility within Hualien’s wider tourism promotion efforts. The county government has continued since 2024 to launch tourism marketing campaigns to attract international and domestic visitors to the region. However, initiatives tend to be concentrated on north Hualien County and Hualien City. A staff member managing tourism affairs at the Guangfu Township Office (光復鄉公所) confirmed to me that while the office is keen to promote Guangfu’s tourism assets, there are currently no county-level initiatives aimed at helping Guangfu boost the industry. Local officials are committed to revitalizing tourism but seemingly lack the resources and funding required to conduct sustained, large-scale promotional efforts. [3] It is understandable that Hualien’s tourism efforts were focused elsewhere while Guangfu was still undergoing extensive physical restoration. With the township now largely cleared, though, there is a stronger case for requesting additional funding from the county or central governments for campaigns that put Guangfu at the center of tourism promotion. A Focused Strategy for Restoring Tourist Confidence With the help of county and central government, a tailored tourism-recovery framework could be coordinated for the township. This could include: More accurate, balanced information on conditions and daily life on the ground. Coordinated travel campaigns and incentives. Investment in tourism infrastructure. First, more widely publicized information on the township’s recovery and travel conditions will help accelerate the shift in perceptions. Clear, sustained, and positive communication about regional safety and accessibility, as well as regular local government broadcasting of daily life and cultural events will rebuild the public’s trust. This includes both earthquake-related safety assurances and post-flood recovery stories. “Many people worry that it is unsafe here. But the government has done a great deal to ensure our buildings are secure. Clearer public information on this would help reassure visitors,” says breakfast shop owner Li Jen-i. [4] “Guangfu has recovered quickly from the floods, and life has largely returned to normal for many residents. We hope that coverage of the township can better reflect that reality,” say Laoye (盧政惠) and Juju (陳慧秋), guesthouse owners of Breadfruit B&B (麵包樹舍). They add: “People forget how accessible and peaceful this part of Taiwan is as a holiday destination.” [5] Indeed, despite media coverage focusing primarily on areas under construction, a notable portion of the township was not touched by the floods. The main tourist attractions remain open here, such as the Matai’an Xinlü Farm (馬太鞍欣綠農園 ), where visitors can learn about the indigenous ecological knowledge of the Amis indigenous people (阿美族) ; and the Guangfu Sugar Factory (光復糖廠 ), which dates back to the Japanese period . Without this information to counter negative news coverage, many continue to assume Guangfu is a no-go zone. Second, to effectively promote the township nation-wide and beyond, Guangfu needs the resources of a coordinated government-backed tourism promotion program. Eye-catching marketing campaigns showcasing the area’s rural charm and scenery could be rolled out on social media and displayed in trains, underground (MRT) stations in cities nationwide, and international airports in both Taiwn and abroad. To provide additional financial incentives for people to visit, subsidized travel packages and discounted transport tickets, akin to Hualien County’s post-earthquake discounts, could be reintroduced and adapted for Guangfu. Image: “Laoye” (盧政惠) and “Juju” (陳慧秋), the proprietors of “Breadfruit B&B” (麵包樹舍) in the town of Guangfu (Hualien County) (July 2026). (Image source: Author’s photograph) If the county’s existing tourism campaigns elsewhere in Hualien County are indeed proving effective, the wheel does not need to be reinvented. Government officials can build on existing initiatives and direct them where the region requires further support. Policy lessons can also be taken from abroad. Following the 2019-2020 bushfires in Australia, tourism hotspots across New South Wales struggled with avalanches of cancellations for months . Similarly, f ollowing the 2016 Kumamoto earthquakes , towns in Japan experienced protracted slumps in tourism. In both cases, government-funded campaigns and incentives helped boost the recovery of the tourism industry, which encouraged people to travel in an ordinary fashion, rather than to see residents solely as victims needing support . Third, travel promotion and incentives in Guangfu could be matched with continued investment in tourism infrastructure. While the township is easy to reach by direct train and car hire is convenient, the government can pursue further investment in a number of transit methods to enhance the township’s accessibility. These include expanding bike hire options, improving bus services, and introducing shuttle buses between local attractions. Taiwan already boasts 84 shuttle bus routes country-wide. Until Guangfu enjoys better transport services, reliance on car travel will create barriers for those who cannot drive or who do not hold driving licenses. Taiwan has a strong track record of strategic tourism promotion and infrastructure development. A clear tourism roadmap would build on the government’s existing strengths, putting its tools to work for a township in need of greater support. Lessons in Post-Disaster Recovery for Taiwan and the World Cases of natural disasters in Guangfu have shown that while physical restoration can take place remarkably quickly, the harder task is ensuring that local industries recover long-term. This experience can offer lessons that extend well beyond Taiwan. As climate change intensifies the frequency and severity of extreme weather worldwide, governments will increasingly be required to consider the protracted effects of these occurrences on local communities. Building strong strategies to ensure long-term recovery is crucial. Taiwan, meanwhile, has particular reasons to strengthen its capacity for resilience. Its exposure to natural disasters, as well as ongoing concerns over geopolitical tensions in the Taiwan Strait, means that the government is constantly contending with international perceptions of a nation in danger. Taiwan needs to be able not only to rebuild industries after crises, but also to continuously reassure visitors that the country remains a safe and appealing destination. Guangfu offers a smaller-scale opportunity to test how strategic information sharing, combined with promotional tourism campaigns and incentives, can help reshape perceptions of a disaster-affected destination. The main point: Effectively reviving a local economy post-disaster and rebuilding its appeal to tourists requires a long-term, targeted approach from government. This includes strategic information sharing, promotional tourism campaigns and incentives, and infrastructure building. This case study of Guangfu, Hualien County—one year after devastating floods—sheds light on the necessary scale of government intervention and the pertinence of strengthening Taiwan’s tourism resilience both regionally and nationally. title: Before the Blockade: Marine Insurance’s Relevance to Taiwan’s Energy Lifeline
zh_title: 封锁前：海上保险与台湾能源生命线的关系
source: 华盛顿全球台湾研究中心
summary: 下载整期 PDF 如果发生台湾海峡危机，运往台中或台湾其他主要港口之一的液化天然气 (LNG) 货物的命运可能会变成一个商业问题：它还能获得战争险吗？由于海军规划受到与潜在封锁相关的大部分关注，因此北约的海事战略或欧盟的经济安全议程几乎没有涵盖海上保险。然而，保险公司的决定可能会像海军部署一样影响台湾。 2026 年发生的事件已经证明了这一点：2 月 28 日罢工之后
content:
下载整期 PDF 如果发生台湾海峡危机，运往台中或台湾其他主要港口之一的液化天然气 (LNG) 货物的命运可能会变成一个商业问题：它还能获得战争险吗？由于海军规划受到与潜在封锁相关的大部分关注，因此北约的海事战略或欧盟的经济安全议程几乎没有涵盖海上保险。然而，保险公司的决定可能会像海军部署一样影响台湾。 2026 年发生的事件已经证明了这一点：2 月 28 日对伊朗发动袭击后，霍尔木兹海峡的航运停止了。没有宣布封锁，但保险公司取消了战争险保险、重新报价或大幅重新定价，流量在一周内下降了 80% 以上。劳合社的数据显示，3 月份仅有 181 艘船只过境，其中大部分与伊朗有关，而冲突前一天有 138 艘船只过境。六个月过去了，交通仍然没有恢复。劳合社情报机构统计，9 月 14 日至 20 日这一周内，有 117 起与伊朗无关的过境事件，比冲突前一天的数量还要少。其后果也影响到了台湾，因为台湾三分之​​一以上的天然气要经过霍尔木兹海峡，而大约 96% 的能源需要进口。虽然台湾一半以上的电力由燃气发电厂提供，但其液化天然气库存只能维持 11 天。
目前，政府要求安全库存为11天，并将在2027年增加到14天。同期存储容量预计将从20天增加到24天。所有三个接收站均位于西海岸，面向中华人民共和国（PRC）。这使得台湾的时间非常短：如果液化天然气输送停止，减载（即计划轮流停电）将在几天内开始，并且还需要电网来支持该岛的防御。图片：台湾高雄永安液化天然气接收站（资料照片日期不详）。 （图片来源：Wikimedia Commons） 海上保险如何关闭台湾海峡 商船通常为船舶投保船体险和战争险，并为船员受伤、污染、残骸清除和第三方损害等责任提供保护和赔偿 (P&I)。银行不会为未投保的船舶提供融资，承租人也不会租用一艘船舶。联合战争委员会 (JWC) 是一家总部位于伦敦的组织，由来自劳合社市场协会和国际承保协会的代表组成，汇集了承保海洋船体战争险的承保人。该委员会公布了一份被认为船只遭受战争相关危险风险增加的地理区域清单。因此，船东必须在进入该区域之前通知其保险公司，而保险公司可能会收取额外的风险保费。
此外，租船合同中的战争风险条款允许船东拒绝航行到所列区域，即使有保险。市场可能会在危机完全发生之前发生变化：2022年2月，在俄罗斯入侵乌克兰之前，JWC将黑海和亚速海添加到其所列区域中，以应对随后确实发生的预期情况。 2023年底红海列入名单后，运营商绕行南非好望角，而不是支付附加费。然而，标准的战争风险措辞会带来更大的后果：如果五个永久性国家中的任何两个之间爆发宣战或未宣战的战争，

【原文 English Original】
DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF In the event of a Taiwan Strait crisis, the fate of a liquid natural gas (LNG) cargo bound for Taichung, or one of Taiwan’s other major ports, could turn into a commercial question: can it still obtain war-risk cover? As naval planning receives most of the attention in relation to a potential blockade, marine insurance is barely covered in either NATO’s maritime strategy or the European Union’s economic security agenda . However, an insurer’s decision could affect Taiwan as much as a naval deployment. Events in 2026 have demonstrated this: After the February 28 strikes against Iran, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz halted. No blockade was declared, but insurers canceled, requoted or sharply repriced war-risk cover, and traffic fell by more than 80 percent in a week. Lloyd’s List data showed just 181 vessel transits in March, mostly Iranian-linked, compared with 138 vessel transits a day before the conflict. Six months later, traffic has still not recovered. Lloyd’s List Intelligence counted 117 non-Iranian-linked transits in the week of September 14–20, fewer than on a single day before the conflict. The consequences also affected Taiwan, since more than a third of its gas goes through Hormuz, and about 96 percent of its energy resources are imported. While gas-fired plants generate more than half of Taiwan’s electricity, its working LNG stocks can only last for 11 days . Currently, the government requires a security s tockpile of 11 days, and will raise it to 14 in 2027 . Storage capacity is expected to rise from 20 to 24 days over the same period. All three receiving terminals are on the west coast, facing the People’s Republic of China (PRC). This leaves Taiwan with a very short clock: If LNG deliveries stop, load shedding (i.e., planned rolling blackouts) would begin within days, and the grid would also be needed to support the island’s defense. Image: The Yongan LNG Terminal in Kaohsiung, Taiwan (undated file photo). (Image source: Wikimedia Commons ) How Marine Insurance Could Close the Taiwan Strait A merchant vessel normally has hull and war-risk insurance for the ship, and protection and indemnity (P&I) for liabilities, such as crew injuries, pollution, wreck removal and damage to third parties. Banks will not finance an uninsured ship, and charterers will not hire one. The Joint War Committee (JWC), a London-based organization with representatives from the Lloyd’s Market Association and the International Underwriting Association, brings together the underwriters who write marine hull war risk. This Committee publishes a list of geographical areas where vessels are considered at increased risk of war-related perils. Thus, shipowners must notify their insurers before entering the zone, and underwriters may charge an extra risk premium. Moreover, war-risk clauses in charter parties allow owners to refuse a voyage into a listed area, even when cover is available. The market can move before a crisis fully materializes: in February 2022, before the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the JWC added the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov to its Listed Areas in response to an anticipated situation that subsequently did materialize. When the Red Sea was listed at the end of 2023, operators diverted around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa, instead of paying the surcharge. However, standard war-risk wording carries a larger consequence: If war, declared or undeclared, breaks out between any two of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council , insurance cover ends automatically. Therefore, a conflict between the People’s Republic of China and the United States over Taiwan would fall within the automatic termination clause of the standard Institute War and Strikes Clauses. France and the United Kingdom could also act as contractual triggers rather than distant observers. Lessons from the Hormuz Strait The Hormuz conflict shows how quickly this can happen. War-risk rates for Gulf transits were at 0.25 percent of hull value pre-conflict, but rose sharply within days. Marine insurers Gard, Skuld, NorthStandard, the London P&I Club, and the American Club issued cancellation notices on March 1. Two days later, the JWC extended the Listed Areas across the Gulf littoral, and maritime traffic collapsed. Underwriters in London pushed back against the claim that insurance had closed the Strait, claiming that insurance cover remained available. Instead, cancellation notices were deemed a contractual way to renegotiate terms. Owners kept ships in port because they feared for the safety of their crews and vessels, not because insurance could not be bought. However, insurance contracts had a political impact on shipping decisions around the world within 48 hours, even though no closure orders were issued. Changing the price and terms of risk was enough to halt maritime traffic without a naval blockade. Washington tried to fill the gap: On March 11, the US International Development Finance Corporation named Chubb as lead underwriter for a USD 20 billion maritime reinsurance facility, expanded to USD 40 billion on April 3. Despite this, the measure had limited effect s: It covered the Strait but not the surrounding waters, and excluded loss of life and environmental damage, liabilities of greatest concern to P&I clubs and shipowners. Image: An interior shot of the Lloyd’s Building in London, headquarters of the maritime insurance conglomerate Lloyd’s of London (Sep. 2014). (Image source: Wikimedia Commons ) Inserting Taiwan into the Marine Insurance Ecosystem Taiwan lacks institutional channels with key decisionmakers. The JWC works with security advisers, officials and shipping companies, but Taiwan has no standing in the process because it is not formally recognized by most European institutions. Despite this, Taiwanese companies Evergreen, Yang Ming, and Wan Hai rank among the world’s larger carriers . However, in the first week of a crisis, private entities acting in their own commercial interests would decide whether LNG carriers keep sailing, as their choice would be based on Beijing’s capacity to exert influence and coercion. This gap does not necessarily imply bad faith from insurers. Governments have used insurance as a tool of coercion for more than a decade: In 2012, the European Union banned P&I cover for Iranian oil cargoes ; and Security Council Resolution 2321 (2016) prohibited insurance for North Korean vessels. Thus, the PRC knows how these mechanisms work. A permanent forum could close the gap. It should bring American, Taiwanese, British, French and Nordic officials together with the JWC, the International Group, and the main war-risk underwriters. The purpose is to ensure that the committee knows what escort plans, port measures and public guarantees are actually available in the Taiwan Strait, rather than relying on signals Beijing sends. It could be based on the example of c ounter-piracy coordination off Somalia , where governments and industry representatives met and the London market adjusted its Listed Areas as conditions changed. Opportunities for US-Taiwan Collaboration The US government also needs a public backstop before a crisis. Senator Pete Ricketts’s Taiwan Energy Security and Anti-Embargo Act , reported out of committee in January 2026, and Representative Pat Harrigan’s companion House bill would authorize the US Maritime Administration to insure foreign-flagged vessels carrying critical goods to Taiwan if commercial cover were withdrawn. Nevertheless, a Taiwan facility would have to cover the approaches, adjacent waters, crew liability, and environmental damage from day one—and not two weeks later, as it happened in Hormuz. This facility would also have to state in advance how public insurance operates when the five-powers clause ends commercial cover, as this cannot be improvised during a quarantine. Taiwan should be part of those preparations, whether or not it is formally recognized: information about terminal resilience, escort plans, and grid capacity would affect an underwriter’s assessment. Taipei could also negotiate in advance with LNG suppliers and their European insurers on the conditions under which deliveries would continue, which is more cost-effective before a crisis. Marine insurance should be part of Taiwan’s agenda when engaging with Europe, alongside semiconductors. Even though insurers and shipowners did not formally acknowledge the closure of Hormuz in 2026, the events that followed made the Strait unusable for most commercial traffic. Taiwan should start coordinating with the committee in London now to establish a strategy ahead of any future contingency. The main point: Decisions by war-risk underwriters in London could halt LNG deliveries to Taiwan before any naval blockade, as the 2026 Hormuz crisis has showed. Taiwan has no channel to the committee that lists high-risk areas, and a war between the United States and the PRC would end commercial cover automatically. Taipei and Washington should open a standing dialogue with the London market now, and define in advance the public insurance that would take over. title: Donate to Support the Contemporary Uyghur Anthology, organized by Uyghur Anthology
summary: The Contemporary Uyghur Anthology is a publication that platforms Uyghur (and anyone drawing their roots from East Turkistan) artists and writers in the diaspora by providing a space that is often inaccessible to those in our community. The
content:
The Contemporary Uyghur Anthology is a publication that platforms Uyghur (and anyone drawing their roots from East Turkistan) artists and writers in the diaspora by providing a space that is often inaccessible to those in our community. There are no other projects of its kind in the English language, and with two volumes already published, we hope to take this project to the next level. It's a rare look at Uyghur expression in an environment where all our stories are told by people pushing their own narratives without the intimate knowledge of our lived experiences.

<"Manifesto" by Sumayah Jurad from Vol. II>

We asked ourselves these questions - why wait for others to invite us to the table when we can pull up a chair and introduce ourselves? Why let others speak for us without trying first to speak? Our broken English can only be improved with audacity, and world literature is only enriched by the presence of new voices.

All-in-all, our efforts have been met with support from our community and pleasant surprise from those who did not know what they did not know.

Somewhat unprecedented is that we publish the authors' original language alongside the translation. Our book is filled with Uyghur, Latin, Cyrillic, and Chinese script to encapsulate as much of our community's experience as we can.

**Our Story**

There are many publications in diaspora communities that platform East and South Asians, SEA, MENA, and more. Central Asia is often underrepresented in world literature or Asia-specific publications, and occupied territories even less so. Uyghurs themselves have been a relatively new diaspora community in English-speaking countries, and haven't had the opportunities to grow their literary or artistic communities. Many don't have the tools to nurture their talents, or knowledge of creative networks or opportunities, even when many journals seek work from underrepresented groups. In instances where they are aware, it's difficult to be published in this competitive field without the education and styles that publications look for. There are only a handful of literary translators translating from Uyghur to English, and not many Uyghurs who have had the chances to develop their creative language when learning English.

To sum up, the issues were:

*   No spaces for Uyghur writers and artists to develop their skills
*   A disconnect from artist communities, be it local or online
*   Lack of awareness of opportunities
*   No bridge between our native tongue and English, and in turn, world literature

So, we put together a small group at the Tarim Network to take on this challenge. Completely volunteer-run; the very essence of a passion project. We did a call-out for anything and all. New writers, established writers, any language, any genre, whatever we could print in a book. And here we were, the first book of its kind, created to speak for ourselves without outsider voices, without a publishing house, raw and straight from the source.

<From the launch of Vol. I at Harvard University>

The blurb from our first volume:

_"The Contemporary Uyghur Anthology is a collection of Uyghur reflections in diaspora. Weaving together memories of the homeland, experiences of displacement, and transitions of identities, this anthology is a creative reflection of the beauty and complexities of the Uyghur experience._

_By centering Uyghur voices at the forefront, this anthology serves as a form of living memory in a pivotal moment of Uyghur history. The title Under the Mulberry Tree refers to a story from the Uyghur literary classic Ana Yurt, where youthful Nuri faces terrible injustices, separation, and turmoil; but for one moment in the Charbagh, his love for Sebihe and his own family is full, ripe, and sweet, like the mulberries from the ancient tree. In a similar way that the mulberry tree offered comforts in Nuri’s time of need, we hope this volume offers a place of reflection and celebration of Uyghur culture."_

We'd partnered with a member from a Jewish organisation to run writing workshops and explain editorial processes, as we had never worked on something like this before. After that collaboration, we decided to publish a revised edition on our own. This time, we added editors' notes to the pages to explain certain terms and historical and cultural contexts - mainly for our own youth, who don't always have access to cultural education. We translated more pieces from Uyghur and Chinese. Our contributors spanned 13 countries, at all levels of experience.

Was this work sustainable? Equipped with the tools, experience, and outpouring of support from our first volume, we spent the next two years saying yes. Our first book was now in libraries, there were articles and academic papers that mentioned it, and most of all, we reaffirmed the need for this sort of work. Not only were we accepting submissions, we worked one-on-one with emerging writers and artists to edit their pieces. We also helped first-time translators have their first publications with help from more experienced translators, as well as connecting them with the original authors.

Our second volume was even better than the last. From the blurb:

"How do we respond to the unexpected, and how does it influence perceptions of ourselves or the environments in which we exist? As a diaspora population, unexpected encounters can shape and transform what it means to be Uyghur as we build a new life outside of the homeland. Encounters Under the Mulberry Tree takes on the literal, abstract, and expanded renditions of these moments. We feature contemporary and historical works, including art, poetry, and prose in five languages with contributors based in a dozen countries, from established writers like award-winning author and filmmaker Tahir Hamut Izgil, to emerging artists, writers and translators of all ages. This book is a library of vignettes that grapple with intersections and how we make sense of it all."

Our stats:

*   44 pieces in total by 36 contributors
*   Five languages (Uyghur, English, Chinese, Russian, Turkish)
*   All work translated into English
*   11 translators
*   Contributors based in over 10 countries

<Vol. II showcased at a college hosted by Rawan Mentorship>

**Volume 3**

Now we embark on our third volume. The three of us do this while maintaining full time jobs, academic careers, and other side projects. We all live in different countries and have only met in person once. But it's something that we need to do, for our community and for ourselves. Our contributors have gained so much from this experience and we want to extend this opportunity to more people. This needs to survive in order for similar initiatives to be born.

**How we'd like to proceed**

*   **Supporting the editors -** all expenses so far have been paid out-of-pocket or through book sales. We do not have any donors or sponsors (yet!).
*   **Supporting our contributors -** we cannot afford to pay any of our contributors. Despite this, we have given free copies of the book to contributors, but this is definitely leaving a dent in our pockets.
*   **Recruiting more people -** paid internships or remuneration for one-off work would help volunteers spend more time on this project in this economy.
*   **Enhance our level of expertise -**we want to improve. Workshops or courses for our editors and contributors, professional feedback, the works. Unfortunately there is no one who speaks Uyghur and who is involved in Western publishing or English literature on a professional or academic level. We would appreciate connections with professionals from any language background, or the funding to level up.
*   **Expand our network -**we'd love to promote our work at literary festivals, go to conferences, do book events, establish ourselves in the public eye, provide reader copies to reviewers, and so on. However, there is a funding barrier to overcome to be able to attend these events, organise, or pre-order books.

<Vol. I on display at the Mosquers Film Festival, 2025>

**Who we are**

**Munawwar Abdulla** is an Uyghur advocate, poet, and scientist born on unceded Kaurna land (Australia) and based in Massachusetts. She co-founded The Tarim Network, runs Uyghur Collective, and collaborates on projects with Uyghur rights organisations around the world. Her writings and literary translations have been published in places such as Modern Poetry in Translation, Asymptote, the Margins, the Georgia Review, and others.

**Sonya Imin** is a mixed Uyghur American scholar and multi-disciplinary creative who has worked on art and film projects across the US, Europe, and Central Asia. Growing up between the borderlands of the Uyghur homeland, broader Central Asia, and the midwestern United States, interrogations of belonging, home, and displacement influence the nature of her work. Currently based in Brussels, she is working on her doctoral research on Uyghur artistic production in the diaspora.

**Maidina Kadeer**is a mixed Uyghur-Hui writer and editor, born in Ghulja and currently based in Montreal (Tiohtià:ke), Canada. She holds a BA in English Literature and Law and Society from Concordia University, with a focus on post- and neo-colonial literature. Her work explores Uyghur identity, history, and culture through cuisine, agriculture, and neo-colonialism. She has contributed to projects such as a poem, NinetySix, in Slavs and Tatars’ Contest of the Fruits (2021) and participates in panels and interviews on Agriculture and Food History to raise awareness about Uyghur culture.

# Help our local Uyghur restaurant!

In 2018, Gairatjan Rozi, a talented Uyghur chef, trained in Europe and now settled in America, opened 'Marco & Polo' in Hyattsville.  The restaurant's menu features the cuisine of his homeland, in the Uyghur Autonomous Region of China, with classic Uyghur dishes including hand-pulled laghman noodles, dumplings, and lamb kebabs, complemented by more familiar Turkish and Mediterranean fare. Within just a few years, Mr. Rozi and his restaurant has earned the love of our community. His food & restaurant has been featured in the local press and has earned a dedicated following in the Washington DC region. Unfortunately the COVID-19 pandemic is forcing Mr. Rozi to close his family-run kitchen, shutter his beloved restaurant, and put in storage his colorful collection of Uyghur artifacts which decorate 'Marco & Polo.' But Mr. Rozi is hopeful. Having dedicated his new life in America to 'Marco & Polo,' he dreams of reopening his restaurant soon - in a new location that will attract even more customers who want to enjoy & explore both the cuisine and the Uyghur culture of Central Asia. Your generous donation to this GoFundMe effort will help Mr. Rozi begin to recover finically from the COVID-19 disaster and allow him to pursue his dream of creating another unique Uyghur dining experience for our community! Rehmet! (Uyghur for 'thank you')www.yelp.com/biz_photos/marco-and-polo-hyattsville-2?

May 8, 2021

Sarah Elder Organizer

Dear Friends of Marco & Polo restaurant - Here is an exciting update on Mr. Rozi's efforts to reopen his wonderful Uyghur restaurant. Due to rising lease prices in Prince George's County and permitting time delays AND an unforeseen opportunity Mr. Rozi will be reopening Marco & Polo Restaurant in Guilford, CT.

 The town of Guildford is situated near Yale University in New Haven, CT. Mr. Rozi has found a welcoming community for Uyghur culture at Yale University. Yale has hosted Uyghur cultural events and will continue to do so. These events connected him with a benefactor who is inviting Mr. Rozi to reopen there much sooner than he is capable to do so in Prince George's County.

 Thanks to this community and many well wishers our GoFundMe has raised over $10K! Mr. Rozi has incurred storage costs and of course, personal costs, as he's navigated the restaurant leasing and county permitting world. And for the curious, contributions are still welcome! (This GoFundMe will remain active for a few more weeks.)

 While we are sad to see Mr. Rozi leave our area, we see this as a win-win. Mr. Rozi's restaurant and dream will continue to thrive and more Americans will continue to learn about Uyghur culture.Read more

# Support Uyghur film & tell the story together

Hello dear friends:  We've been making preparation for this film for nearly a year. It is a story of a young Uyghur man’s life in exile after losing contact with his family members. We have received funding from a few organizations, but not quite enough for the entire production process. So we decided to ask for help from those of you who care about the Uyghurs and the work that we’re doing. Our goal is to reach $10,000.  If you have any interest in Uyghur culture or the Uyghur film industry, then please consider a contribution. Your small act of kindness will greatly enhance this film, you will not be disappointed. This film will open your eyes to stories from a beautiful and marginalized people group  The film will be released on March 21st, 2023. All donors will be listed in the end credits and receive a steamable/ download link to the film, and donors who give $100 or more contributions will receive special thanks and additional gifts as shown below:  $100 donation - you will receive a physical copy of the film and a handwritten thank you letter. $200 donation - you will receive a physical copy of the film, a poster with the director’s signature and a handwritten thank you letter. $500 donation - you will receive a physical copy of the film, a poster with the director’s signature and a handwritten thank you letter also your name will be present on the director's special thanks section ending of the film. $5000 donation - you will receive all of the above and will be credited as a co-producer. Ï Summary  Shirzat, an Uyghur international student who has just graduated from college in the United States, had big dreams for his future prior to undertaking his education. He had planned to return to his homeland to take over his father's business, marry his long-term girlfriend, build a happy family, and become a successful entrepreneur. But with the sudden implementation of China's arbitrary mass abduction policy, millions of Uyghurs, like his father, were taken and have disappeared. For Shirzat, who wasn’t able to pursue his studies due to the crisis back home, this was tragic. He felt he had been thrown from the sky to the ground. With finances in ruins, his father missing, his family in danger, his relationship hanging by a thread, he soon spiraled into a cloud of depression and compulsive attention to politics. He withdrew from his relationships with his friends and put his life on hold while struggling to overcome his painful reality and searching for hope in the midst of it.  Our team  We will work with some of the most talented people around the world. The Director and screenwriter of this film have decades of experience in the industry. He has also made a number of short films while in university, many of which won the best picture of the year at regional and international film festivals. Our core team members are creative-minded people who have participated in numerous film projects. We have absolute confidence that we will work together as one and give the audiences astonishing results.

A Book about Anti-Communist Movies

We are on the eve of the announcement of the lineup at the first annual Anti-Communist Film Festival. Our headline film is **The Lives of Others.**

I’ve spent over a year talking to Hollywood studios about licensing, visiting movie theaters to make my case (as you might expect, some were not thrilled with the idea), and finally getting a sponsor with the great folks at the Victims of Communism Foundation.

**There’s one more thing I’d like to do. I have a 20,000-word essay about my favorite anti-communist movies, and I'd like to publish it next year as a book and companion to the film festival.** Excerpts from the essay have been published on Hot Air, Chronicles, and on the Victims of Communism website. I’d like to publish the entire essay in paper format, something that people can hold. A samizdat, which during the Cold War was a book or pamphlet that was forbidden in communist countries and was passed around from hand to hand by dissidents.

**Most importantly, what I am calling Freedom’s Fury: A Guide to Anti-Communist Movies would be something that cannot be digitally erased.**

In his forthcoming book Reds: A Global History of Communism, journalist Paul Mason explores how communists want us to forget the past:

I do not want to “take control” of the memory of Marx, any more than the memory of the Russian Revolution or the Spanish Civil War. But I do want to prevent the Communist Party of China from taking control of them. Because, as [philosopher Walter] Benjamin reminds us: “not even the dead are safe from the enemy.” Just as postwar fascism fought to expunge the facts about the Holocaust, we are now seeing—in Putin’s Russia, Xi’s China, and political movements aligned to them in the global south—systematic distortions of the events described here. And it will get worse. In occupied Ukraine, new statues of Lenin are being erected. In Russia, plaques commemorating victims of the Great Purge are being torn down, and the last museum of the Gulag has been closed. In China, all critical writing about Mao is dismissed as “historical nihilism.”

Mason then notes how his own book may be censored:

As you read each chapter, I want you to imagine how it might be written in a future dominated by the brain-frozen clichés of Chinese communism. The Beijing propaganda machine has been busy eradicating the truth about the Tiananmen Square Massacre for nearly forty years. What might it achieve if given the unchallenged right to curate the facts about 1848, 1917, or indeed 1789? Far from being yesterday’s problem, the struggle for the truth about the history of communism may have only just begun. If so, Benjamin’s words on the eve of its darkest and finest hours bear repeating: Every line we succeed in publishing today—no matter how uncertain the future to which we entrust it—is a victory wrested from the powers of darkness.

**American communists would like nothing more than to censor the Anti-Communist Film Festival and forget it ever existed, even before it begins.**
