title: Steven Gruzd met alleged killers at Airbnb, court hears
summary: Almost seven months after the murder of senior researcher [Steven Gruzd](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2026-03-30-steven-gruzds-murder-highlights-express-kidnapping-spike-as-suspects-appear-in-court/), court details indicate he me
content:
Almost seven months after the murder of senior researcher [Steven Gruzd](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2026-03-30-steven-gruzds-murder-highlights-express-kidnapping-spike-as-suspects-appear-in-court/), court details indicate he met his assailants at an Airbnb in Corlett Gardens, Johannesburg, which they had booked and paid for, and where the murder allegedly took place.

Gruzd (53) was the head of the African Governance and Diplomacy Programme at the South African Institute of International Affairs (SAIIA). He was reported missing on Friday, 27 March, after he had left to attend a meeting in Corlett Gardens.

His body was found the following day at George Goch Hostel in Jeppestown, 20km away. A postmortem determined the cause of death to be blunt force trauma to the neck.

Five men were arrested on the day Gruzd’s body was found. Thabiso Ngcongco, Nkosenhle Zuma, Siyanda Mzolo, Buhle Zuma, and Nsikelelo Njali are facing charges of robbery with aggravating circumstances, kidnapping, murder, and defeating the ends of justice. They have all pleaded not guilty.

The George Goch Hostel, where the body of Steven Gruzd was found. (Photo: OJ Koloti / Gallo Images)

On Friday, 16 October, at the Johannesburg Central Magistrates’ Court, Lieutenant Colonel Johan Potgieter testified that the suspects’ fingerprints were found at the murder scene and inside a white Toyota Corolla driven by the assailants.

The police also found bloodstained linen from the murder scene and a rope with Gruzd’s DNA in the car. CCTV evidence showed the suspects and Gruzd entering the premises separately.

The case has been investigated as a suspected “express kidnapping”. This refers to a crime in which victims are held against their will while being forced by their assailants to withdraw cash from multiple ATMs and send cash transfers to other accounts.

These incidents are [the main driver](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2026-03-30-steven-gruzds-murder-highlights-express-kidnapping-spike-as-suspects-appear-in-court/?dm_source=blocks-horizontal&dm_medium=card-link&dm_campaign=inform&dm_position=4) of kidnappings in Gauteng, which records the highest kidnapping cases nationally.

Steven Gruzd speaking at the African Peer Review Mechanism. (Photo: X / @APRMorg)

The circumstances behind the death revealed in police evidence and through a Daily Maverick investigation point to an alarming trend in express kidnappings, about which LGBT+ activists have been raising the alarm since 2023.

The SA Police Service did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

### Possible links to online gangs

The police have not officially established how the accused and Gruzd knew each other, and they do not appear to have had an established relationship.

A Johannesburg resident, who requested anonymity, told Daily Maverick that he had matched with Gruzd on Grindr, a dating app for men who have sex with men. He confirmed that Gruzd, whom he also knew outside of the app, was “very active” on the site and regularly confided in him.

This detail, along with the circumstances of his murder, points to the possible involvement of criminal syndicates that create fake accounts on Grindr to lure men who have sex with men to secluded locations for robbery and extortion.

Associates of Gruzd have described him as a “devoted family man” to his wife and children.Daily Maverick was not able to reach his family for comment.

### ‘Grindr gangs’ documented since 2023

The online targeting of men who have sex with men is often linked to “Grindr gangs”. However, the term describes the tactic rather than a single, interconnected syndicate. Such gangs have been documented [in Nelson Mandela Bay](https://iol.co.za/news/2025-09-15-beaten-robbed-and-dumped-gay-men-lured-on-grindr-in-new-wave-of-attacks/), [Durban](https://www.mambaonline.com/2026/07/23/four-men-jailed-for-grindr-gang-kidnappings-and-robberies-in-ballito-umhlanga-and-durban-north/)and [Cape Town](https://iol.co.za/capeargus/news/2023-03-15-concern-over-grindr-gang-luring-sa-victims-on-hook-up-app-to-rob-assault-them/).

In 2023, seven men targeted a Wits University student on Grindr before [kidnapping and torturing](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2023-09-22-wits-kidnapping-police-probe-dozens-of-similar-cases/) him, demanding a R30,000 ransom from his family. Police rescued the student from Denver Men’s Hostel after arresting one of the captors while he attempted to withdraw the ransom money.

At the time, SAPS spokesperson Athlenda Mathe stated that the suspects were linked to [at least 85 similar cases](https://x.com/AthlendaM/status/1704764064017068135?s=48&t=PJpBansSH7jGLH5lIBJspQ).

This year, at least two similar incidents in Gauteng were reported. In early March, [Mamba Online](https://www.mambaonline.com/2026/03/02/community-alert-grindr-gang-attack-reported-in-randburg-johannesburg/) reported that a 43-year-old man was ambushed in a guesthouse by five men after he had agreed to meet a Grindr match.

His assailants forced him to hand over his phone, transferred money out of his bank account, tied him up, and threatened to publish explicit photos of him on social media if he “did anything stupid”.

In April, veteran emergency services worker [Braam Kruger](https://www.timeslive.co.za/news/south-africa/2026-05-22-pretoria-guesthouse-murder-three-suspects-from-kzn-granted-bail/)was murdered after being lured to a guesthouse in Brooklyn, Pretoria, by a [Grindr match](https://www.mambaonline.com/2026/05/25/fears-pretoria-guest-house-murder-may-be-linked-to-grindr-gang-criminals/). After he arrived, he was ambushed by three men, robbed and murdered.

Braam Kruger. (Source: Facebook)

The Johannesburg resident who knew Gruzd told Daily Maverick that he knew of at least one other incident where a man in a relationship with a woman went to meet a Grindr match only to be ambushed at gunpoint.

Details of such attacks are widely shared through informal community whisper networks, prompting some men to carry firearms for protection during initial in-person meetups with people they match with on the app.

He added that Grindr automatically erases message history for both users when one account blocks another – a feature that can further complicate criminal investigations.

Grindr had not responded to Daily Maverick’s questions by the time of publication.

The "Grindr" app logo is seen amongst other dating apps on a mobile phone screen. (Photo by Leon Neal/Getty Images)

### Cases underreported due to stigma

Sibonelo Ncanana-Trower, the co-chair of the National Task Team on Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity, Gender Expression, and Sex Characteristics Matters, confirmed a rise in “Grindr gang” incidents, particularly in Gauteng and Cape Town. He noted, however, that the true scale of the problem is probably underreported due to stigma and fear of being outed.

“Our significant concern is that the reported cases likely represent only a fraction of what is actually occurring. Many individuals are extremely fearful of opening cases with the police due to the risk of further harm, secondary victimisation, or being outed, especially in contexts where stigma and discrimination remain pervasive,” he said.

Mike Bolhuis. (Photo: mikebolhuis.co.za.)

### Sextortion on the increase

Private investigator Mike Bolhuis said he had observed a marked increase in sextortion cases across various dating platforms in recent months. In cases handled by his team, offenders routinely set up fraudulent, anonymous profiles to engage and exploit potential victims.

Perpetrators either coerce victims into sending explicit photos to use for blackmail, or lure them to private locations where they are ambushed, held captive, and extorted for money. In physical attacks, the criminals also take explicit photos of the victims, threatening to post them online if they contact the police – and frequently reselling them on the black market.

Bolhuis urged those who use dating sites to verify the identity of the person they have matched with before meeting in person by asking for full names and contact information.

“Because it’s a social media platform, you go through all the necessary other available platforms to find [their profiles]. The moment the person says he’s from overseas, it's a red flag,” he warned.

“When they start asking for money, it’s a red flag. If they don’t want to do a video call, it’s a problem. If they say, ‘Yeah, but I’m in the bath now, I don’t have any clothes,’ and you say, ‘I’ll hold on, put some clothes on.’ You know they come with stories,” he said. **DM**

title: Gold, ancient store of wealth, is finally gaining digital traction
summary: The digital gold market, worth about $50-billion today, is set for liftoff and could tap a swelling vein of demand to reach $700-billion, according to a new report by the World Gold Council (WGC) and Boston Consulting Group. Digital gold pr
content:
The digital gold market, worth about $50-billion today, is set for liftoff and could tap a swelling vein of demand to reach $700-billion, according to a new report by the World Gold Council (WGC) and Boston Consulting Group.

Digital gold provides exposure to the precious metal through digital platforms, eliminating the cumbersome logistics and settlement headaches associated with physical gold.

“As trading and record-keeping has moved onto electronic systems and markets have become more connected, investors have begun to expect gold to behave like other modern assets,” says the WGC.

Traction is building on this front, bringing one of humanity’s oldest stores of wealth into the digital age.

### Token gesture

“Momentum is already building as financial markets undergo a broader digital transformation, bringing tokenised investment products increasingly into the mainstream,” says the WGC.

“Tokenised gold, one segment of the digital gold market alongside vaulted digital gold, has grown fivefold in value since late 2024 to around $6-billion. Cumulative spot trading volumes in tokenised gold exceeded $90-billion in the first quarter of 2026, more than in the whole of 2025.”

This is still small potatoes. The current gold market is worth about $30-trillion at current prices and is focused on jewellery, bars, coins, gold-backed ETFs, OTC5 and central bank reserves. The physical investment gold market is worth about $13-trillion.

The report sees digital gold growing to about $165-billion in the next five years, a figure that could reach $275-billion over the same timeframe if various barriers are removed.

Source: World Gold Council.

“What holds investors back is not a lack of interest but four key barriers: trust, access, utility and cost. Trust is the swing factor. Investors point to stronger consumer protections, transparent proof of backing, accessible redemption and clearer regulation as the conditions most likely to increase confidence in digital gold,” the WGC says.

Access, meanwhile, is hampered by a lack of platforms outside of big Asian markets.

> “Where digital gold is embedded in mainstream channels such as super-apps, payment platforms and banking apps, as seen in India, China and Indonesia, penetration is up to seven times higher than in markets where such distribution does not yet exist.”

The potential for a $700-billion market stems from “latent demand” – a pool of untapped investors who would rather do things in the digital space because this is the 21st century.

“Among today’s digital gold investors, 52% held no gold before their first digital purchase, of which 92% have since bought other forms of gold,” says the report.

Gold has been a red-hot commodity over the past few years and while it is off its historic peaks of almost $5,600 an ounce scaled in January this year, its price remains elevated at more than $4,000 an ounce.

### Performance enhancing

A range of factors explain this performance, including geopolitical uncertainty – which enhances the precious metal’s safe-haven status – and central bank purchases, notably in emerging markets as the greenback loses some of its lustre as the world’s reserve currency.

The digital gold market itself is unlikely to move the dial much on this front but is seen as an entry point into the wider bullion market, especially for younger investors who are obviously more wired than their older counterparts.

Source: World Gold Council.

“Around 65% of latent demand comes from people who have not yet invested in gold. Among those who already hold gold in other forms, more than half would fund a digital gold investment with money not currently allocated to the asset.

“Rather than cannibalising demand for bars, coins or gold-backed ETFs, digital gold is thus likely to attract new investors, and new money,” the report says. **DM**

title: Will Xi, Trump, Putin meet at Apec? First, they must agree on an agenda
zh_title: 习近平、特朗普、普京会在亚太经合组织上会面吗？首先，他们必须就议程达成一致
summary: 尽管美国总统唐纳德·特朗普表示他愿意在[亚太经合组织会议上与中国和俄罗斯同行习近平和弗拉基米尔·普京坐下来](https://www.scmp.com/news/us/article/3371428/trump-says-hes-open-xi-putin-meeting-china-nuclear-talks?module=inline&pgtype=article)峰会](https://www.scmp.com/topics/asia-pacific-economic-cooperation-apec?module=inline&pgtype=article)，目前还很难确定三位领导人是否会在几周内真正会面。观察人士表示，很大程度上取决于各国能否就议程达成一致，一位专家将此描述为“危机”
content:
尽管美国总统唐纳德·特朗普表示他愿意在[亚太经合组织会议上与中国和俄罗斯同行习近平和弗拉基米尔·普京坐下来](https://www.scmp.com/news/us/article/3371428/trump-says-hes-open-xi-putin-meeting-china-nuclear-talks?module=inline&pgtype=article)峰会](https://www.scmp.com/topics/asia-pacific-economic-cooperation-apec?module=inline&pgtype=article)，目前还很难确定三位领导人是否会在几周内真正会面。

观察人士表示，很大程度上取决于各国能否就议程达成一致，一位专家将其描述为“关键杠杆”。

专家表示，如果三边会议举行，俄罗斯将获益最多，因为这次峰会将成为俄罗斯国际孤立正在结束及其大国地位的有力象征。虽然特朗普将证明他可以与其他大国打交道，但这可能会让美国盟友感到不安。

人们一直在猜测，预计将出席在[中国深圳]举行的亚太经合组织峰会(https://www.scmp.com/news/china/politics/article/3371206/chinas-shenzhen-ready-host-xi-trump-and-putin-during-apec-summit?module=inline&pgtype=article)的三位领导人是否会在场外进行前所未有的静坐。
普京早些时候表示，他“完全支持”(https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3370170/kremlin-aide-visits-china-amid-speculation-about-pottial-xi-putin-trump-meeting?module=inline&pgtype=article)”举行三边会议，但他补充说，议程必须明确。 “[三方会议]当然是可能的。在很大程度上，这将取决于中国作为活动的东道主，”他说。

周一，特朗​​普还表示他对此类会谈持开放态度。但他表示，这“对乌克兰来说意义不大”，而且这样的会议必须“以无核化为基础”，而北京长期以来一直拒绝就这一问题进行谈判。

在他发表上述言论之前，《华尔街日报》周一报道称，普京提出三方会谈，作为通过谈判结束乌克兰战争的一种方式，目前乌克兰战争已进入第五个年头。

08:56

习近平为何在中国接待世界领导人而不是出国看望他们

据《南华早报》了解，中国官员私下里对三方会谈的想法表示欢迎，但并未积极推动。也很少有关于议程或筹备工作的实质性讨论。

当周一和周二被问及对三边会议的可能性发表评论时，中国外交部发言人毛宁表示，她没有可提供的信息。
中国人民大学重阳金融研究院院长王文表示，议程将为任何峰会定下基调，并决定其成功与否。

“议程是会议能否真正举行的关键杠杆，”王说。

“如果三个政党的私人议程存在冲突，或者他们提议的主题根本不一致，那么会议就不太可能举行。

“只有当议程聚焦于共识领域，同时避开‘红线’……对话才有可能成为可行的可能性。”

华盛顿智库昆西研究所的丹尼斯·西蒙对此表示同意，认为这三个国家存在“利益重叠”，但没有“共同的战略愿景”。

他补充说，虽然[核问题](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/mi

【原文 English Original】
While US President Donald Trump has said he is [open to sitting down](https://www.scmp.com/news/us/article/3371428/trump-says-hes-open-xi-putin-meeting-china-nuclear-talks?module=inline&pgtype=article) with Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin at the [Apec summit](https://www.scmp.com/topics/asia-pacific-economic-cooperation-apec?module=inline&pgtype=article), it remains far from certain that the three leaders will actually meet in a few weeks.

Observers said much would depend on whether the countries could agree on an agenda, with one expert describing this as a “critical lever”.

Russia was set to gain most if the trilateral meeting took place, experts said, as the summit would be a potent symbol that the country’s international isolation was ending and of its great-power status. While Trump would get to show he could deal with the other powers, this could unsettle US allies.

Speculation has been building over whether the three leaders, who are all expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the [Chinese city of Shenzhen](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/politics/article/3371206/chinas-shenzhen-ready-host-xi-trump-and-putin-during-apec-summit?module=inline&pgtype=article), will hold an unprecedented sit-down on the sidelines.

Putin earlier said he was “[all for](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3370170/kremlin-aide-visits-china-amid-speculation-about-potential-xi-putin-trump-meeting?module=inline&pgtype=article)” a trilateral meeting but added that the agenda had to be clear. “[A trilateral meeting is] certainly possible. To a large extent, this will depend on China as the host of the event,” he said.

On Monday, Trump also signalled he was open to such talks. But he said it would be “not so much for Ukraine” and that such a meeting would have to be “based on denuclearisation”, an issue Beijing has long resisted negotiating.

His comments followed a Wall Street Journal report on Monday that said Putin floated the three-way talks as a way to negotiate an end to the Ukraine war, now in its fifth year.

08:56

Why Xi Jinping is hosting world leaders in China instead of travelling abroad to see them

The South China Morning Post understands that Chinese officials have privately welcomed the idea of three-way talks, but have not pushed aggressively for them. There has also been little substantive discussion of an agenda or preparations.

When asked on both Monday and Tuesday to comment on the possibility of a trilateral meeting, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said she had no information to provide.

[Wang Wen](https://www.scmp.com/author/wang-wen?module=inline&pgtype=article), dean of the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University, said the agenda would set the tone for any summit and determine its success.

“The agenda is the critical lever for whether a meeting can actually take place,” Wang said.

“If the three parties harbour conflicting private agendas or if their proposed topics are fundamentally misaligned, the meeting is highly unlikely to happen.

“Only when the agenda focuses on areas of consensus while steering clear of ‘red lines’ … can a dialogue become a viable possibility.”

Denis Simon of the Quincy Institute, a Washington think tank, agreed, arguing that the three countries had “overlapping interests” but did not share a “common strategic vision”.

He added that while the [nuclear issue](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3356269/china-adds-warheads-nuclear-powers-walk-away-disarmament-sipri?module=inline&pgtype=article) offered the most obvious potential starting point, Ukraine, trade, Taiwan and the broader international order would inevitably enter any conversation.

Hemant Adlakha of Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi said that “without a clearly agreed-upon agenda, the possibility of the trilateral [talks] happening in Shenzhen is rather remote”.

He suggested that, in the absence of a formal meeting, the three leaders might instead opt for a more informal encounter, perhaps a “stroll together or a cup of tea”.

Lyle Goldstein of Defence Priorities, a Washington think tank, said the agenda might determine whether the potential gathering was “short and symbolic or alternatively lengthy or substantive”. He argued that Trump’s meetings with Xi and Putin had been “helpful overall in cooling world tensions”.

Wang said Beijing would be keen to discuss issues that were global, constructive and mutually beneficial, such as the risks inherent in major-power relations, the global economic recovery, food and energy security and climate change.

But Beijing would resist any pressure to align with a particular bloc as well as “unfair proposals” such as “forcing China into US-Russia nuclear arms control negotiations”.

“[China is] open to discussing mutually beneficial cooperation, but issues concerning [its] sovereign rights are off the table, and any demand to ‘take sides’ is a non-starter,” he added.

Beijing has long refused to join trilateral arms control talks with Washington and Moscow, arguing that its nuclear arsenal does not match up to those of the US and Russia. China is thought to have hundreds of warheads, while the Russian and American stockpiles are in the thousands.

[Cui Hongjian](https://www.scmp.com/topics/cui-hongjian?module=inline&pgtype=article), head of European Union studies at Beijing Foreign Studies University, said the thaw in Washington’s ties with both Beijing and Moscow had laid some groundwork for a meeting, but that stability would need to be maintained for talks to go ahead.

He pointed to uncertainty over the [Ukraine war](https://www.scmp.com/topics/ukraine-war?module=inline&pgtype=article), which he said was weighing on the US-Russia relationship, and to the trade tensions between Washington and Beijing.

“To bring about a three-way meeting, I think an important precondition is that each of the bilateral relationships stays stable, with no major reversals or changes,” he said.

Trump open to nuclear talks with Xi and Putin

Cui said the political will of the three sides would also be decisive. The Trump administration, in particular, would first need to weigh how a meeting fitted its domestic politics, including the looming midterm elections, before committing fully to talks on the agenda, he said.

Sergey Radchenko, a Chinese and Russian foreign policy specialist at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, said a meeting of the three powers would give Russia a chance to “separate the US from its European allies” and hand the Kremlin political leverage while bolstering its status as a great power.

He expected Ukraine to be on the agenda if a meeting took place, with Russia pushing for an end to the war. He also said China’s presence could open the door to talks on security guarantees that would bind Beijing to any settlement.

But he doubted that Xi “will necessarily be enthused by the idea of such a summit”.

“He and Putin have previously cooperated in trilateral formats. However, this is a proposition of a completely different order, and perhaps it is a format that Xi will find difficult to handle,” he said.

Simon offered a more granular reading of the three leaders’ incentives. Trump, he said, would see the meeting as “an opportunity to demonstrate his ability to deal directly with the world’s other two major powers, without being constrained by traditional alliances”.

For Putin, simply sitting at the table would be a diplomatic victory, ending Russia’s isolation and giving him a platform to discuss Ukraine, whereas Xi is likely to be the most cautious, according to the Quincy Institute’s Simon.

“Xi would welcome the recognition of China as an indispensable global power, but would be cautious about becoming part of an arrangement that legitimises American and Russian spheres of influence at China’s expense,” he said.

Cui suggested that if the meeting went ahead next month, it would send a positive signal that the three major powers shared a desire to promote global stability and development.

Beijing, as host, would stand to gain by showing its sense of international responsibility, he said.

“Objectively speaking, this meeting offers China primarily symbolic value, with substantive gains playing a secondary role,” Wang added.

“Symbolically, this is where its greatest value lies. It reaffirms China’s status as a global hub, demonstrating that no major international issue can be advanced without China’s participation. It underscores China’s role as a core force for balancing relations between major powers and stabilising the international order.”

But such a meeting could unsettle US allies, including European countries and Japan, according to Wang. He said a trilateral dialogue would deepen “strategic anxiety” in Europe and Japan since both had long shaped their foreign policies around the US’ stance in great-power rivalries.

If such talks became regular, he said, it would mark the end of a “global order defined by bloc-based confrontation” and could potentially leave US allies such as Europe and Japan in “a state of strategic disorientation, compelling them to re-evaluate their own positions on the global stage”.

However, Goldstein argued that seeing the trilateral as “bad news” for Japan and Europe amounted to a “zero-sum worldview”, and that having such meetings regularly could inspire other sets of three-way talks, including between Europe, Russia and the US or alternatively China, Japan and the US.

Also, Adlakha said, the trilateral meeting might “severely” test China’s efforts to maintain a careful balance between supporting Putin and [preserving ties with Europe](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3371217/china-warns-eu-not-fantasise-trade-approach-brussels-confirms-new-kill-switch?module=inline&pgtype=article).

But Wang played down expectations, suggesting that a meeting would at most produce a crisis communication channel to prevent strategic miscalculation, a basic consensus on global issues and clearer “red lines” for each side.

“Any expectation that such a meeting could resolve the Russia-Ukraine conflict or fundamentally reshape the global order is entirely unrealistic,” he said.

content:
查尔斯顿号航空母舰 (LCS-18) 航行于南海，2023 年 2 月 5 日。美国海军照片

菲律宾马尼拉——据北京称，查尔斯顿号航空母舰(LCS-18)“非法侵入”南海争议海域周边地区后，周二被中国军队追踪。

解放军表示，周二早些时候，中国军队被派往萨比纳浅滩附近监视独立级濒海战斗舰。中国根据其十段线领土主张对该海域拥有主权。

解放军南部战区在一份声明中表示：“美方行为侵犯中方主权权益，危害海上安全，不利于地区和平稳定。美方应立即停止此类活动。海南战区部队始终保持高度戒备，坚决维护国家主权安全，维护地区和平稳定。”

自[2024年与马尼拉对峙](https://news.usni.org/2024/09/14/manila-withdraws-coast-guard-flagship-from-sabina-shoal-ais-shows)以来，中国人民解放军海军、中国海警快艇和中国海上民兵船只一直维持北京在萨比纳浅滩的存在。这些行动是由中国在南沙群岛前沿部署的大型部队来维持的，该群岛拥有多个填海造地的陆地基地，配有机场、港口、传感器以及防空和反舰导弹系统。
美国航行正值中国和菲律宾之间一个月的紧张局势加剧之际。自10月初以来，两国在南海和吕宋海峡至少发生了[8次近距离接触](https://news.usni.org/2026/10/09/philippine-and-chinese-incidents-spike-in-south-china-sea-luzon-strait)。

美国海军军舰和海岸警卫队快艇通常部署到南海进行航行自由行动。去年，一艘中国海军导弹驱逐舰与中国海警巡逻艇严重相撞，导致两名中国水兵丧生，[USS_Higgins_ (DDG-76)]在黄岩岛举行了航行自由行动](https://news.usni.org/2025/08/13/navy-denies-china-chased-off-u-s-warship-from-scarborough-shoal)死了。

美国第七舰队前沿部署的濒海战斗舰定期在南海巡逻并与东南亚国家进行演习。 7月和8月，美国“圣巴巴拉”号航母（LCS-32）连续与菲律宾、日本和澳大利亚军队在整个地区进行海上合作活动。海军 [P-8A 海神](https://news.usni.org/2023/10/06/another-summer-in-the-south-china-sea-a-guided-tour-of-the-worlds-most-contested-waters) 和海军陆战队 [MQ-9A收割者](https://news.usni.org/2024/06/03/u-s-marine-mq-9a-reapers-now-deployed-to-the-philippines)也在这些航行期间提供情报、监视和侦察支持。
[！[图片 2：Aaron-Matthew Lariosa](https://news.usni.org/wp-content/uploads/userphoto/337.jpg)](https://news.usni.org/author/amlariosa)

### [亚伦-马修·拉里奥萨](https://news.usni.org/author/amlariosa)

亚伦-马修·拉里奥萨 (Aaron-Matthew Lariosa) 是一名自由国防记者。他的报道重点是菲律宾国防现代化、南海和美国在第一岛链的努力。
[关注@AaronMatthewI_L](https://twitter.com/@AaronMatthew_L?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

【原文 English Original】
USS Charleston (LCS-18) navigates the South China Sea, Feb. 5, 2023. US Navy photo

MANILA, Philippines — USS _Charleston_ (LCS-18) was tracked by Chinese forces on Tuesday after the ship “illegally intruded” into the area surrounding a contested South China Sea maritime feature, according to Beijing.

Chinese forces were dispatched to monitor the Independence-class LCS near Sabina Shoal early Tuesday, the PLA said. China claims the maritime feature under its 10-Dash Line territorial assertion.

“The U.S. action infringes upon China’s sovereign rights and interests, jeopardizes maritime security, and is detrimental to regional peace and stability. The U.S. side should immediately cease such activities. Forces of the STC remain on high alert at all times to resolutely safeguard national sovereignty and security and uphold regional peace and stability,” the People’s Liberation Army Southern Theater Command said in a statement.

The PLA Navy, China Coast Guard cutters and China Maritime Militia vessels have maintained Beijing’s presence at Sabina Shoal since a [2024 standoff with Manila](https://news.usni.org/2024/09/14/manila-withdraws-coast-guard-flagship-from-sabina-shoal-ais-shows). These operations are sustained by a large forward-deployed Chinese force in the Spratly Islands, which is host to several reclaimed land bases with air fields, ports, sensors and anti-aircraft and anti-ship missile systems.

The U.S. sail comes amid a month of heightened tensions between China and the Philippines. Since the beginning of October, at least [eight close encounters](https://news.usni.org/2026/10/09/philippine-and-chinese-incidents-spike-in-south-china-sea-luzon-strait) have occurred across the South China Sea and Luzon Strait between the two countries.

U.S. Navy warships and Coast Guard cutters usually deploy to the South China Sea for Freedom of Navigation Operations. Last year, [USS _Higgins_ (DDG-76) held a FONOP](https://news.usni.org/2025/08/13/navy-denies-china-chased-off-u-s-warship-from-scarborough-shoal) at Scarborough Shoal in the aftermath of a severe collision between a PLAN guided-missile destroyer and CCG patrol vessel that left two Chinese sailors dead.

Forward-deployed LCSs under U.S. 7th Fleet regularly patrol the South China Sea and drill with Southeast Asian states. In July and August, USS _Santa Barbara_ (LCS-32) held consecutive maritime cooperative activities with Philippine, Japanese and Australian forces throughout the region. Navy [P-8A Poseidon](https://news.usni.org/2023/10/06/another-summer-in-the-south-china-sea-a-guided-tour-of-the-worlds-most-contested-waters) and Marine Corps [MQ-9A Reapers](https://news.usni.org/2024/06/03/u-s-marine-mq-9a-reapers-now-deployed-to-the-philippines) also provide intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance support during these sails.

# Bougainville Needs a Credible Timetable for PNG’s Independence Vote. Australia Can Help.

Canberra should stay out of what Port Moresby decides on Bougainville, but it can push for a concrete timeline for the decision.

By **Yilan Liang**

October 20, 2026

[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?url=https%3A%2F%2Fthediplomat.com%2F2026%2F10%2Fbougainville-needs-a-credible-timetable-for-pngs-independence-vote-australia-can-help%2F&title=Bougainville+Needs+a+Credible+Timetable+for+PNG%E2%80%99s+Independence+Vote.+Australia+Can+Help. "Share on LinkedIn")[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fthediplomat.com%2F2026%2F10%2Fbougainville-needs-a-credible-timetable-for-pngs-independence-vote-australia-can-help%2F "Share on Facebook")[](https://bsky.app/intent/compose?text=Bougainville+Needs+a+Credible+Timetable+for+PNG%E2%80%99s+Independence+Vote.+Australia+Can+Help.%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fthediplomat.com%2F2026%2F10%2Fbougainville-needs-a-credible-timetable-for-pngs-independence-vote-australia-can-help%2F "Share on Bluesky")[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Bougainville+Needs+a+Credible+Timetable+for+PNG%E2%80%99s+Independence+Vote.+Australia+Can+Help.&url=https%3A%2F%2Fthediplomat.com%2F2026%2F10%2Fbougainville-needs-a-credible-timetable-for-pngs-independence-vote-australia-can-help%2F "Share on X")

PNG Prime Minister James Marape (right) and Bougainville’s President Ishmael Toroama hold up the Melanesian Agreement, which recognized the legitimacy of the 2019 independence referendum, June 26, 2025.

Credit: [Facebook/ Autonomous Bougainville Government](https://www.facebook.com/photo.php?fbid=1144492431052655&set=pb.100064757263193.-2207520000&type=3)

In September, Kokoda constituency in Bougainville declared itself [“independence ready.”](https://www.pnghauslain.com/toroama-congratulates-kokoda-constituency-for-being-independence-ready/) At the ceremony, Ishmael Toroama, president of the Autonomous Bougainville Government, pledged funding for a hospital and a police station.

[Similar ceremonies](https://www.nbc.com.pg/post/22632/tonsu-independence-ready) are being held across Bougainville, an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea (PNG). Each carries the same message: the long road from civil war to self-determination is nearing its end.

97.7 percent of Bougainvilleans [voted in favor of independence](https://www.pmnec.gov.pg/prime-minister-marape-and-president-toroama-conclude-historic-jsb-consultations-clearing-way-for-bougainville-referendum-results-to-be-tabled-in-parliament/) in 2019, but that referendum was not binding. PNG’s parliament has the final say, and seven years later, the wait for a parliamentary decision continues.

This year, Prime Minister James Marape had proposed holding a vote on [August 30](https://www.pmnec.gov.pg/prime-minister-marape-emphasises-constitutional-pathway-for-bougainville/). Parliament [formally received the result](https://www.pmnec.gov.pg/png-bougainville-to-meet-in-october-to-set-date-for-parliament-vote-on-referendum-result/) on August 27, then adjourned without voting.

Now Peter Tsiamalili Jr, Bougainville’s regional MP and the leader of government business, has [announced a two-day debate for October 20-21](https://www.thenational.com.pg/mps-given-2-days-to-debate-referendum-results/). That is progress. But it remains unclear whether the sitting will end in a vote, or what will follow if parliament adjourns without one.

Australia has been careful on the issue of Bougainville, with good reason. In 2022, Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said Canberra’s job was to [“support Papua New Guinea.”](https://www.minister.defence.gov.au/transcripts/2022-10-13/joint-press-conference-papua-new-guinea-parliament-house-port-moresby) Bougainville’s leadership took that [as a retreat from neutrality](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-10-16/bougainville-president-responds-richard-marles-independence/101540014), and Canberra had to clarify that it would support whatever the two sides agreed.

Australia is right to keep its distance on what parliament decides, but it can – and should – help nudge PNG to make a decision.

The [2001 Bougainville peace agreement](https://abg.gov.pg/uploads/documents/BOUGAINVILLE_PEACE_AGREEMENT_2001.pdf) required a referendum within 10 to 15 years after the election of Bougainville’s first autonomous government. The agreement also gave PNG’s parliament authority to make the final decision on independence – but did not set a deadline for parliamentary action.

The [2022 Era Kone Covenant](https://www.peaceagreements.org/agreements/2605/) set 2027 as the outer limit for implementing independence or another settlement, but again it failed to fix a date for parliament to vote. The covenant’s one interim deadline – tabling the result in parliament by the end of 2023 – was missed by almost three years.

The lack of a deadline lets Port Moresby postpone a politically difficult decision; meanwhile Bougainville’s leaders must keep persuading supporters to accept the wait. Many who sustained the peace are former combatants who staked their credibility on the promise that politics would produce an answer. Toroama himself was once a rebel commander. He now warns that [trust is under strain](https://islandsbusiness.com/news-break/bougainville-presses-for-self-government-by-2027-independence-by-2030/) even as he urges Bougainvilleans to stay patient. Each postponement makes that appeal harder to sustain.

The approaching PNG election compounds the problem. Under the [provisional timetable](https://www.thenational.com.pg/bougainville-included-in-ge27-chief-sec/), voting will be held

title: Lithium Africa weighs $60M offer for Springbok lithium project

summary: Lithium Africa (TSX-V: LAF) (FSE: 6MQ) (OTCQB: LTAFF) 已收到其南非 Springbok 锂项目的两项非约束性融资要约，其中包括一项 6,000 万美元的投资提案，该项目的目标是在 2027 年下半年首次生产。其中一项要约将通过与承购相关的预付款机制支持近期锂辉石精矿的生产，而另一项要约将资助全地区范围内的勘探和建设更大的加工厂。 “我们正在运行一个竞争流程，我们现在的工作是选择能够为 L 带来最大价值的合作伙伴和结构
content:
Lithium Africa (TSX-V: LAF) (FSE: 6MQ) (OTCQB: LTAFF) 已收到其南非 Springbok 锂项目的两项非约束性融资要约，其中包括一项 6,000 万美元的投资提案，该项目的目标是在 2027 年下半年首次生产。其中一项要约将通过与承购相关的预付款机制支持近期锂辉石精矿的生产，而另一项要约将资助全地区范围内的勘探和建设更大的加工厂。 Lithium Africa首席执行官Thomas Benson博士在一份声明中表示：“我们正在进行竞争性流程，我们现在的工作是选择能够为Lithium Africa股东带来最大价值的合作伙伴和结构，以便Springbok的小规模生产能够为整个地区的大规模勘探提供资金。”这些提案可以为非洲锂业提供一条生产途径，同时减少其筹集额外资金的需求。该公司表示，将继续与 20 多家潜在交易对手就承购、预付款、供应商融资和项目级股权安排进行讨论。周二上午，Lithium Africa 股价在多伦多上涨 11.7%，至每股 1.62 加元，该公司估值为 4,040 万加元（合 2,800 万美元）。第一份报价来自一家大型国际商品培训机构，将提供预付款便利，以换取 Springbok 生产前三年 100% 的锂辉石精矿。
锂辉石精矿是生产锂的主要原材料，对于电动汽车和能源存储系统至关重要。第二个报价来自一家由财富世界 500 强集团支持的锂加工公司。它将投资 6000 万美元，来自一家由财富全球 500 强集团支持的锂加工公司。它将投资一家新控股公司 55% 的权益，该公司将持有 Lithium Africa 在 Namli Exploration & Mining (Pty) Ltd 中 70% 的权益，该公司持有 Springbok 项目。此次交易意味着该项目 100% 的投资前估值约为 7000 万美元。 Lithium Africa 将保留新控股公司 45% 的股份，根据 1.09 亿美元的隐含融资后估值，其价值约为 4900 万美元，但无需为 6000 万美元的计划做出贡献。在拟议的资金中，大约 1000 万美元将用于整个 Springbok 地区的钻探，其余 5000 万美元用于建设加工厂。 Benson 表示：“收到一家大型贸易公司和一家锂加工公司的报价表明了人们对 Springbok 的浓厚兴趣，Springbok 是一个获准开采的矿山，有望在 2027 年投产。”开发时间表 Springbok 项目是在该公司与中国锂生产商赣锋锂业的子公司 GFL International Co., Ltd. 50/50 的合资企业之外进行的。
该公司计划在 2027 年上半年做出融资决定，随后进行建设，但须获得批准并完成融资。这两项要约均不具有约束力，Lithium Africa 警告称，不能保证其将以可接受的条件完成融资，或者根本无法保证。

【原文 English Original】
Lithium Africa (TSX-V: LAF) (FSE: 6MQ) (OTCQB: LTAFF) has received two non-binding financing offers for its Springbok lithium project in South Africa, including a $60-million investment proposal, as it targets first production in the second half of 2027. One offer would support near-term spodumene concentrate production through an offtake-linked prepayment facility, while the other would fund district-wide exploration and construction of a larger processing plant.  “We are running a competitive process, and our job now is to select the partner and the structure that deliver the most value for Lithium Africa shareholders, so that small-scale production at Springbok can fund large-scale exploration across the district,” Lithium Africa CEO Dr. Thomas Benson said in a statement. The proposals could provide Lithium Africa with a path to production while reducing its need to raise additional capital. The company said it continues discussions with more than 20 potential counterparties over offtake, prepayment, vendor financing, and project-level equity arrangements. Shares in Lithium Africa were up 11.7% to C$1.62 apiece on Tuesday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at C$40.4 million ($28 million).  The offers   The first offer comes from a major international commodity training house and would provide a prepayment facility in exchange for 100% of Springbok’s spodumene concentrate in its first three years of production.   Spodumene concentrate is the primary raw material to produce lithium, essential for electric vehicles and energy storage systems.  The second offer comes from a lithium processing company backed by a Fortune Global 500 group. It would invest $60 million comes from a lithium processing company backed by a Fortune Global 500 group. It would invest for a 55% interest in a new holding company that would hold Lithium Africa’s 70% interest in Namli Exploration & Mining (Pty) Ltd, which holds the Springbok project.   The transaction implies a pre-money valuation of approximately $70 million for 100% of the project.  Lithium Africa would retain 45% of the new holding company, valued at approximately $49 million based on an implied post-money valuation of $109 million, without contributing to the $60 million program.  Of the proposed funding, approximately $10 million would go toward drilling across the Springbok district, with the remaining $50 million for a processing plant.  “Receiving offers from both a major trading house and a lithium processing company shows the strength of interest in Springbok, a permitted mine with a path to production in 2027,” Benson said.  Development timeline   The Springbok project is held outside the company’s 50/50 joint venture with GFL International Co., Ltd., an affiliate of Chinese lithium producer Ganfeng Lithium.   The company aims to make a financing decision in the first half of 2027, with construction to follow, subject to approvals and completion of financing.   Neither offer is binding, and Lithium Africa cautioned that there is no guarantee it will complete financing on acceptable terms, or at all.

title: Examining State-Level Legislation on Transnational Repression in the United States
summary: Transnational repression has become an increasingly visible public policy issue in the United States, and worldwide, over the past decade. The gruesome 2018 [murder](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-45812399) and dismemberment of Saudi
content:
Transnational repression has become an increasingly visible public policy issue in the United States, and worldwide, over the past decade. The gruesome 2018 [murder](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-45812399) and dismemberment of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in the Saudi Consulate in Istanbul, the 2023 [assassination](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jul/08/murder-canada-sikh-activist-hardeep-singh-nijjar-indian-criminal-gang-leader-charged) of Canadian Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar outside of a British Columbia temple, and the 2025 [rendition](https://www.frontlinedefenders.org/en/case/one-year-after-his-arrest-human-rights-defender-hugues-comlan-sosoukpe-remains-custody) of Beninese journalist [Comlan Hugues Sossoukpè](https://cpj.org/data/people/comlan-hugues-sossoukpe/) from Côte d’Ivoire highlight the extent to which governments have brazenly targeted their nationals across borders.

Initially, the policy response in the United States occurred entirely at the federal level. But over the past several years, U.S. states have begun to consider legislation on the issue. Not all of this legislation has been adopted, and the U.S. state-level response is clearly in an early phase. As U.S. states continue to respond to transnational repression, it is important that state legislators – and ultimately, members of Congress – understand what the states have done and what can be learned from their various approaches.

One of the challenges of countering transnational repression is that it has not yet been defined in U.S. federal law. The democracy and rights organization [Freedom House](https://freedomhouse.org/report/transnational-repression), which has played a leading role in drawing attention to the issue and in gathering data on it, defines transnational repression as “governments reaching across [national] borders to silence dissent among diaspora and exile communities.” (One of us, Grady, is a research analyst at Freedom House.) Perpetrator governments employ a range of tactics – including assassinations, illegal deportations, abductions, digital threats**,**and coercion-by-proxy – to intimidate and harass those who pose a perceived threat to the regime. Transnational repression can also involve the abuse by authoritarian regimes of legitimate international legal cooperation mechanisms such as [Interpol’s notice system](https://newlinesinstitute.org/intl-law-peace/how-the-abuse-of-interpol-contributes-to-transnational-repression/), [mutual legal assistance frameworks](https://www.ohchr.org/en/statements-and-speeches/2026/09/joint-statement-united-nations-human-rights-experts-transnational) and [counterterrorism financing structures](https://carnegieendowment.org/russia-eurasia/politika/2025/11/russia-eu-banking-exploits).

## **The Federal Response**

The federal response to transnational repression in the United States has been [varied](https://newlinesinstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/FINAL_TNR-US_policy-report-nlisap.pdf). Numerous congressional committees have held hearings — including multiple hearings by the U.S. Helsinki Commission and most recently, and relevantly, the Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC) June 4, 2026, [hearing](https://www.cecc.gov/events/hearings/prcs-threats-americans-transnational-repression-state-level-responses) on “The PRC’s Threats to Americans: Transnational Repression & State-Level Responses.” Federal law enforcement has regularly brought cases against perpetrators, and U.S. congressional offices have introduced several bills on transnational repression, including the [Transnational Repression Policy Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/2525/text) (TRPA). Yet, that bipartisan and bicameral legislation, which would codify a formal definition of the phenomenon into law and mandate the development of a government strategy to blunt the threat, has struggled to move on the Hill, given other legislative priorities.

U.S. administrations have also evaded the intent of the most significant U.S. legislation, Section 6503 of the 2022 National Defense Authorization Act, entitled “Transnational Repression Accountability and Prevention” or “[TRAP](https://www.congress.gov/117/plaws/publ81/PLAW-117publ81.pdf).” The provisions directed the Attorney General and Secretary of State to provide biannual reports to Congress on authoritarian governments’ misuse of Interpol’s systems, support reforms to prevent such abuse, and develop a coordinated U.S. response to this form of transnational repression. While the required [initial report](https://www.state.gov/transnational-repression-accountability-and-prevention-trap-act-reports) was submitted in August 2022, the TRAP provisions have not produced the sustained reporting, coordinated implementation, or broader accountability that Congress envisioned. The result is that, while the U.S. federal government has done more than any other government to raise awareness about transnational repression, its response has been neither unified nor consistent.

Indeed, the United States and other democracies continue to [facilitate](https://freedomhouse.org/report/special-report/2026/collaboration-and-resistance-tracking-transnational-repression-2025) transnational repression via their immigration and extradition systems by detaining and deporting dissidents. Part of the challenge is that, precisely because of the widespread participation of democracies in international legal cooperation, it is all too easy for perpetrator governments to abuse these systems to seek the return of exiled activists and dissidents. While those mechanisms require greater transparency and stronger safeguards against abuse, receiving countries must also ensure that they do not detain, extradite, or deport individuals based solely on uncorroborated allegations or requests from governments with a documented history of abusing these systems for political purposes.

By the same token, a great deal of transnational repression occurs outside of immigration enforcement, in the everyday lives of those targeted. Adhering to due process standards when adjudicating claims for asylum, while essential, will not protect individuals from surveillance, harassment, coercion, or intimidation by foreign regimes or their agents inside the United States. These are acts that can be addressed at the state level. Indeed, given the federal structure of the United States, leaving every offense to the federal government to criminalize is neither sensible nor safe. U.S. states, in addition to serving as legislative laboratories, can play a constructive role in responding to the challenge of transnational repression.

## **State Legislative History and Legal Mechanisms**

In recent years, state legislatures have increasingly taken steps to address foreign interference. In general, legislative initiatives have been broad, treating transnational repression, alongside land sales and [foreign lobbying campaigns](https://www.akingump.com/en/insights/alerts/state-level-foreign-influence-laws-begin-taking-effect), as increasingly serious national security concerns. These broad approaches have prompted some concerns about the potential for overreach. At a June hearing of the U.S House of Representatives Select Committee on China, the president of Asian Americans Advancing Justice, John C. Yang, [cautioned](https://www.congress.gov/119/meeting/house/119385/witnesses/HHRG-119-ZS00-Wstate-YangJ-20260625.pdf) that efforts to address foreign interference must avoid repeating historical instances of national security concerns leading to ethnicity-based suspicion rather than evidence-based enforcement.

Since the beginning of 2025, seven states have adopted laws that explicitly mention transnational repression and enact measures to respond to the phenomenon. While these laws vary to some extent in scope and approach, they reflect growing state-level attention to the problem.

In May 2025, Texas became the first state to pass legislation to counter transnational repression. [Senate Bill 1349](https://legiscan.com/TX/text/SB1349/id/3235301), signed into law by Governor Greg Abbott on May 24, 2025, and effective on September 1, 2025, criminalizes actions committed by a foreign government or terrorist organization, or an agent working on behalf of these entities, when the acts interfere with Texas residents’ protected conduct under the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution or in some way coerce a Texas resident to either work for a foreign principal or to [leave the United States](https://safeguarddefenders.com/en/blog/new-report-chasing-fox-hunt). The law also makes it illegal to enforce another country’s laws in the state. The sentencing enhancement for serving a foreign principal can be applied to pre-existing offenses in the Texas penal code, including assault, stalking, and human trafficking. The law also requires the Texas Department of Public Safety to create a training program for Texas law enforcement on common tactics and on the primary perpetrators of transnational repression, and requires the Department, in collaboration with the Governor’s office, to prepare a study on the issue.

While the law identifies how transnational repression infringes on the rights of affected individuals, it takes an overly expansive view of the perpetrators by including terrorist organizations. Unlike terrorist offenses, which usually attack state institutions or the public at large, government-directed campaigns are targeted against particular private individuals who, as individuals, have the rights the law seeks to protect. Moreover, the act incorrectly implies that terrorist organizations stably control territory and are recognized foreign principals.

Soon after Texas passed its law in 2025, Nebraska adopted the [_Crush Transnational Repression in Nebraska_](https://nebraskalegislature.gov/FloorDocs/109/PDF/Slip/LB644.pdf)[_Act_](https://nebraskalegislature.gov/FloorDocs/109/PDF/Slip/LB644.pdf). It defines transnational repression as actions committed by a foreign government or terrorist organization, or an agent working on behalf of these entities, “with the intention of harassing, intimidating, censoring, or otherwise extending such principal’s ability to influence, control, or impose such principal’s preferences on the behavior of individuals outside of the principal’s territory or jurisdiction.” Similarly to the Texas measure, the Nebraska law introduces a criminal sentencing enhancement for covered offenses — including first-, second- and third-degree assault, stalking, and violation of a harassment protection order, among others — that interfere with Nebraskans’ protected conduct under the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution or that seek to force a Nebraska resident to work for a foreign principal or leave the United States.

In addition to these increased penalties, the act calls on Nebraska State Patrol to create training on cross-border repression tactics and key perpetrators, to establish a website with a multilingual reporting mechanism for targeted individuals, and to prepare a report for the legislature. Certainly, training and multilingual reporting tools are helpful. However, the legislation’s repeated reference to the term “foreign adversary” may increase the likelihood that the implementation process will only focus on governments like China and Iran and overlook transnational repression linked to U.S. allies such as [Saudi Arabia](https://www.ohchr.org/en/press-releases/2019/06/khashoggi-killing-un-human-rights-expert-says-saudi-arabia-responsible) and [India](https://apnews.com/article/india-nikhil-gupta-pannun-sikh-murder-b1c6a424dc2bfc4d8606d08ba70b00c6).

Laws in [Arizona](https://www.azleg.gov/legtext/57leg/1r/laws/0224.htm) (2025), [Kansas](https://www.kslegislature.gov/b2025_26/bills/hb2413/) (2026), [Louisiana](https://www.billtrack50.com/billdetail/1981650) (2026), and [Tennessee](https://www.billtrack50.com

content:
## Critical Minerals and Energy Intelligence

[News](https://theoregongroup.com/)>[Latest News](https://theoregongroup.com/latest-news/)>China to restrict exports of mine-building tunnel machines

*   China will require licences for exports of tunnel boring machines (TBMs) and their key parts to “sensitive” countries from November 18, under [an October 19 Commerce Ministry and customs announcement](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn/zwgk/zcfb/art/2026/art_9ce34ccfa6c040d7a4f7622f89133be5.html)
*   Chinese manufacturers account for [nearly 70% of the global TBM market](https://en.people.cn/n3/2025/0605/c90000-20323751.html), and market leader China Railway Hi-tech claims [85% of China’s TBM market at non-coal mines](https://payneinstitute.mines.edu/china-dominates-the-market-for-machines-that-open-mines/)
*   the rules also cover cutterheads, main drives, remanufacturing technology and [wet-shotcrete machines built for work above 3,000 metres](https://www.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202610/19/WS6ad6327be4b06d4aa05639f8.html)

China has added tunnel boring machines to its dual-use export control list, extending the licensing approach it has used on [rare-earth magnets](https://theoregongroup.com/commodities/rare-earths/chinas-rare-earth-magnet-exports-to-us-fall-21-before-trump-xi-summit/) to the heavy equipment that builds underground mines.

The rules take effect on November 18. They cover shield and hard-rock TBMs, plus cutterheads, screw conveyors, segment erectors, main drive systems and the technology used to remanufacture them.

Exports to “sensitive countries and regions” in disputes with China will need a licence. Shipments elsewhere will go through a registration system, but exporters and end users must promise not to pass Chinese-made machines on to those destinations. Beijing has not said which countries count as sensitive.

That leaves a lot of buyers exposed as Chinese manufacturers account for [nearly 70% of the global TBM market](https://en.people.cn/n3/2025/0605/c90000-20323751.html), exporting about [US$793 million of rock cutters and tunnelling machinery in 2025](https://mining.com.au/china-commerce-ministry-announces-export-controls-for-tunnel-boring-machines/).

China’s exports of US$793 million worth of HS 843031 tunnelling machinery in 2025 is about seven times what the US exported last year, at roughly [US$109 million](https://comtradeapi.un.org/public/v1/preview/C/A/HS?reporterCode=842&period=2025&cmdCode=843031&flowCode=X&partnerCode=0); although note, the code also includes coal and rock cutters.

### The mining angle

Much of the early coverage has focused on [India’s metro, rail and border tunnels](https://www.thehindu.com/news/international/china-imposes-export-controls-on-tunnel-boring-machines-sought-by-india-citing-national-security/article71602536.ece). But TBMs are increasingly used to cut declines and [access tunnels at mines](https://payneinstitute.mines.edu/china-dominates-the-market-for-machines-that-open-mines/). For example:

*   Chinese manufacturer CRCHI shipped a [5.63-metre mining TBM to Zambia’s Chambishi copper mine](https://www.tunnelsandtunnelling.com/news/crchi-exports-mining-tunnel-boring-machine-tbm-to-africa/) to bore a 9.7-km tunnel for a US$830 million project
*   Anglo American drove an [exploration tunnel of about 8.1 km](https://payneinstitute.mines.edu/china-dominates-the-market-for-machines-that-open-mines/) towards its Los Sulfatos copper prospect in Chile, finishing in 2011, and Codelco agreed in 2022 to trial a mining TBM with Komatsu
*   Ivanhoe Electric plans to start boring a [4-km decline at its Santa Cruz copper project](https://www.ivanhoeelectric.com/news/ivanhoe-electric-to-acquire-robbins-tunnel-boring-machine-and-material-handling-system-for-mine-access-development-at-the-santa/) in Arizona in the third quarter of 2027

Ivanhoe Electric’s executive chairman, Robert Friedland, has already said the controls won’t hold up Santa Cruz as its machine comes from Ohio-based Robbins, in a [package costing about US$64.7 million](https://www.ivanhoeelectric.com/news/ivanhoe-electric-to-acquire-robbins-tunnel-boring-machine-and-material-handling-system-for-mine-access-development-at-the-santa/) that includes refurbishment and a material-handling system.

“Over the past 20 years, Chinese-produced TBMs have grown from ZERO to 60-70% of the global market share,” Robert Friedland [wrote on X](https://x.com/robert_ivanhoe/status/2112126428653203466). “So, we suspect that this news will cause a PANIC in the global TBM market.”

Notably, the rules reach beyond new machines: rebuilt TBMs are common in mining outside China, and controls on cutterheads, main drives and remanufacturing technology give Beijing [a say over the rebuild cycle as well as new sales](https://payneinstitute.mines.edu/china-dominates-the-market-for-machines-that-open-mines/).

Chinese groups have also [bought up Western TBM technology](https://payneinstitute.mines.edu/china-dominates-the-market-for-machines-that-open-mines/), including France’s NFM, Aker Wirth’s TBM intellectual property and Caterpillar’s former Lovat business in Canada. Even Robbins was [61% owned by China’s NHI from 2016](https://www.worldconstructionnetwork.com/analysis/robbins-reborn-8694522/) until industry veteran Lok Home [bought back substantially all its assets](https://www.robbinstbm.com/announcement/), in a deal announced in February 2021.

### Why the impact may be limited

This is a licensing regime, however, not an embargo, with China’s Commerce Ministry [saying it will approve applications that meet the rules](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn/xwfb/xwfyrth/art/2026/art_1e581b3d58ff46dabe8c44abab408d6c.html) — and Chinese makers need foreign orders.

For example, CRCHI’s overseas revenue rose to [a record 32.4% of its main-business revenue in the first half of 2025](https://payneinstitute.mines.edu/china-dominates-the-market-for-machines-that-open-mines/).

TBMs also remain a niche tool in mining. For example, at Montana’s Stillwater platinum and palladium mine, TBMs have historically cost [about a third as much to run as a conventional mining fleet](https://www.worldconstructionnetwork.com/analysis/tbms-advance-on-mines/), but needed about 1.5 times the capital.

The more likely result, [as the Payne Institute argues](https://payneinstitute.mines.edu/china-dominates-the-market-for-machines-that-open-mines/), is longer lead times and a standing option for Beijing to slow deliveries to particular countries.

But, the timing still matters. Copper miners are already struggling to add supply, as we explained in our earlier article [Refined copper surplus forecast, but copper mines struggle to keep up](https://theoregongroup.com/latest-news/coppers-104000-tonne-surplus-masks-continued-mine-supply-constraint/):

> “The forecast therefore relies on project execution, but the ICSG has already cut 2026 mine growth twice, from the 2.3% it expected in October 2025 to 1.6% in April and 1.3% now.”

Any further disruption, however marginal, threatens to tighten long-term supply further.

The controls don’t stop any mine from being built, but they give Beijing influence over how fast some of the West’s new underground copper supply gets dug.

title: The End of a Dream: Can International Sanctions Dismantle Authoritarian Rule in Georgia? - EST
summary: ## **Abstract** In response to Georgia’s political crisis of late 2024 and ongoing democratic backsliding, several Western nations imposed targeted sanctions against ruling party Georgian Dream’s (GD) officials and billionaire founder Bidzi
content:
## **Abstract**

In response to Georgia’s political crisis of late 2024 and ongoing democratic backsliding, several Western nations imposed targeted sanctions against ruling party Georgian Dream’s (GD) officials and billionaire founder Bidzina Ivanishvili. The article evaluates whether existing restrictions can meaningfully reverse democratic backsliding in Georgia and reinvigorate the country’s Euro-Atlantic integration. Drawing on an academic literature review of sanctions effectiveness against non-democratic regimes, the analysis characterises Georgia as an emerging personalist autocracy, whose elites can be responsive to a targeted or “smart” sanctioning model. “Smart” sanctions can undermine regimes’ elite appeasement and dissent-suppression capacity without triggering a “rally-around-the-flag” effect, which makes them strategically optimal for sender states. Furthermore, an analysis of the United States’ Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) framework concludes that despite a robust legal framework consisting of aggregation, extraterritoriality, and secondary sanctions principles, critical vulnerabilities such as the issuance of enabling general licenses, lack of cooperation between major sanctioning authorities (US, UK, and the European Union), and delayed action can jeopardise sanctions impact against the GD. In order to maximise impact, the Western coalition must close legal loopholes, coordinate restrictions, and target selection in the time window before full authoritarian consolidation in Georgia.

Keywords: International sanctions, sanctions effectiveness, autocracy, smart sanctions, Georgian Dream

## Georgia in Turmoil

Georgia has been in a deep political crisis since late 2024, following the October Parliamentary elections, which local and international observers criticised for widespread procedural violations (Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights, 2024). The government’s subsequent suspension of EU integration until 2028 only amplified public discontent (Civil Georgia, 2024b). The ensuing protest demonstrations have been violently dispersed, leading to detentions, imprisonment, and heavy fines targeting activists, journalists, and opposition politicians (Transparency International Georgia, 2025a). In response to the crackdown, the United States, the United Kingdom, Ukraine, the Baltic states, the Czech Republic, and Germany imposed personal sanctions on officials of the ruling Georgian Dream (GD) party, the Ministry of Internal Affairs (MIA), the judiciary, pro- governmental media personalities, and entrepreneurs (Transparency International Georgia, 2025b). Sanctions involved travel bans and asset freezes, though the latter were applied in only a minority of cases. The European Union agreed to suspend visa-free entry for holders of diplomatic passports (Council of the European Union, 2025). GD’s founder and honorary chair, Bidzina Ivanishvili, remains the most high-profile person sanctioned. This article examines the academic literature on the effectiveness of sanctions against non- democratic regimes. For this analysis, effectiveness is determined by whether or not sanctions can compel the Georgian government to reverse democratic backsliding and return the country to its Euro-Atlantic path. Using the United States’ sanctions architecture as a case study, the article reviews current restrictions and analyses ways in which the international community can leverage them against the GD most effectively.

## **Sanctions: Effective or Useless**

According to the critical literature review by Peksen (2019), the effectiveness of economic or financial sanctions can be examined from two primary perspectives – those of the sanctioning (sending) and sanctioned (target) states. The sender-based school of thought holds that effective sanctions generally require inflicting (or threatening) substantial damage on the target by weaponizing the target’s political and economic ties to the sender (Peksen, 2019). However, such pressure may be ineffective if the target can bypass sanctions, either through alternative trade partners or illicit channels (von Soest, 2023). To limit circumvention possibilities, sanctions can be imposed by a coalition of states or international organizations (e.g., the United Nations and the European Union are considered more effective (Peksen, 2019). Likewise, the effectiveness of sanctions in the Georgian context will likely depend on the sender states’ ability to sufficiently pressure the GD, while also restricting circumvention options. The target-based school of thought, on the other hand, assumes that the outcomes of sanctions depend on the target state’s political system. Two crucial factors influencing compliance are the leadership’s ability to (1) shield their elites from the adverse effects of restrictions and (2) suppress dissent among the population (Peksen, 2019). Given limited public accountability, non-democratic regimes are expected to be less compliant than democracies when sanctioned (Zarpli, 2022). Autocracies can divert tax or trade revenues to reimburse the elites’ financial losses without public scrutiny. Meanwhile, the loyal security apparatus suppresses popular dissent (Zarpli, 2022). However, different types of autocracies manage the effects of sanctions with varying degrees of success. For instance, personalist autocracies might be more vulnerable due to low institutionalization, limiting their opportunities to appease elites and suppress dissent. In addition, dependence on external aid also makes such regimes more likely to concede under pressure (Peksen, 2017). Conversely, single-party or military dictatorships are more resilient since their control over state institutions and the public is more entrenched (Peksen, 2017). Within this framework, Georgia can be characterised as an emerging personalist autocracy, given the informal leadership of Mr. Ivanishvili and the ongoing democratic backsliding (Zedelashvili et al., 2025). For sanctions senders, this means that Georgian elites can be vulnerable to economic pressure, even though the possibility of regime transformation towards a more institutionalised autocracy can diminish the effect of sanctions. The literature also distinguishes between comprehensive and targeted or “smart” sanctions (Drezner, 2022). Comprehensive sanctions, such as trade embargoes, target the nation’s economy as a whole, while “smart” sanctions only pressure public officials and regime loyalists such as media personalities, entrepreneurs, etc. (von Soest, 2023). The GD and its associates have thus far been exposed to targeted travel and financial sanctions, which are generally considered more effective against autocracies (Peksen, 2019). This assumption rests on the fact that affected individuals or groups possess influence over state policies and, thus, can lobby for their amendment if pressured by sanctions (von Soest, 2023). The second reason relates to narrative control in authoritarian regimes (Grauvogel & Von Soest, 2014). Since comprehensive sanctions (such as trade embargoes) can cause standards of living to decline, the authorities can frame them as an attack against the nation and consolidate public support against the sanctions senders (Drezner, 2022). By sidestepping domestic pressure in such a way, autocrats can minimise the effectiveness of sanctions (Grauvogel & Von Soest, 2014). In contrast, smart sanctions are less susceptible to such framing due to their limited scope.

## **Sanctions and Elite Appeasement**

Although the overall evidence does not indicate a systematic effort, so far there have been several attempts by the Georgian public authorities to reward the sanctioned officials for their loyalty (Civil Georgia, 2025). In one instance, the Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze promoted Vakhtang Gomelauri, then Minister of Internal Affairs (MIA), to one of his Deputies (Civil Georgia, 2024e). President Mikheil Kavelashvili awarded Gomelauri and his colleague Zviad Kharazishvili, the head of the “riot police”, with the Order of Honour (Civil Georgia, 2025). While authorities have extensively shielded law enforcement from allegations of brutality (Civil Georgia, 2024d), both Gomelauri and Kharazishvili resigned from their MIA posts months after being sanctioned by the United States and the United Kingdom. Despite the scarcity of evidence, restrictions can potentially affect GD’s elite appeasement capacity. In Georgia’s case, this capacity largely rests on Bidzina Ivanishvili, sanctioned by the US in December 2024 (U.S. Embassy in Georgia, 2024). Ivanishvili is the wealthiest person in the country, with a net worth of 2.7 billion USD (Forbes, 2025). Local and international human rights watchdogs have been criticising him for exercising informal control over the government by placing close associates in key positions (Transparency International Georgia, 2020). Allegations also underscore his supposed direction of the MIA response to the 2024 anti-government demonstrations (Civil Georgia, 2024c). Utilising the “smart” approach to sanctions, thus making Ivanishvili’s personal and family assets the primary targets of restrictions, could undermine his credibility among the GD loyalists as the guarantor of wealth and privileges. Without sufficient resources to buy or reward loyalty, Ivanishvili may struggle to protect his support coalition from external pressure, contributing to the effectiveness of sanctions (von Soest, 2023). The US’ Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) restrictions well illustrate the opportunities and limitations of sanctions against Ivanishvili and the GD. Administered by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), SDN sanctions freeze the US-based assets of targeted individuals or businesses and deny access to the American financial system, including third- party transactions in US dollars, severely restricting Ivanishvili’s capacity to support his elites. Targeted individuals also face entry bans under SDN sanctions (Hess, 2024). OFAC can authorise exemptions from certain sanctions regimes by issuing general or specific licences. Aside from these exceptions, non-compliant individuals or enterprises may face fines, criminal prosecution, or sanctions of their own (Hess, 2024). SDN sanctions are particularly effective due to the principles of aggregation and extraterritoriality (Hess, 2024). The aggregation principle allows OFAC to block any enterprise in which a sanctioned individual owns at least 50% of the shares. If several targeted individuals jointly own 50% or more of the shares, the enterprise can still be sanctioned (Hess, 2024). This provides an opportunity to increase pressure on Ivanishvili by extending sanctions to the companies he co-owns or will own in the future. But so far, a general licence exempts Ivanishvili’s businesses from this rule, only banning business with his person (Office of Foreign Assets Control, 2024). OFAC generally warns against engaging with enterprises connected to sanctioned persons, since restrictions may always be extended to the former (Office of Foreign Assets Control, 2020). However, the leeway created by the general licence likely allowed Ivanishvili to transfer ownership of his assets from offshore companies in Belize and Panama to associated Georgian enterprises (Transparency International, 2025e). Similarly, the absence of British sanctions against Ivanishvili reveals another weakness, as major assets rest in the UK overseas territories, which also act as offshore jurisdictions (Transparency International Georgia, 2025f). These cases demonstrate why an effective sanctions architecture must seal legal loopholes and have broad multilateral support. Neither condition is fully met for the GD-related restrictions at the moment, jeopardizing effectiveness. ZUNYI, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- Zunyi in southwest China's Guizhou Province has a resonant title: the "city of historic turning point."

In January 1935, an enlarged meeting of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee was held in Zunyi during the Long March. The Zunyi Meeting is regarded as a crucial turning point of the Long March, leading to the ultimate success of the Chinese revolution. Since then, Zunyi has become a sacred place for generations of CPC members, and the footprints of the Red Army are forever imprinted on the city's culture and spirits.

Rooted in its revolutionary past, the city is now embarking on a new chapter of development while retaining its historical significance.When the Red Army passed through, its population stood at just over 30,000. By 2025, the permanent population of its central urban area exceeded 1.6 million, with an urbanization rate of 61 percent.

Zunyi also calls for developing new quality productive forces in light of local conditions and accelerating the building of a modern industrial system.

The year 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March. Take a drone tour above China's "city of historic turning point."
